Protecting Kids from Lead: Federal Leaders Visit Philadelphia Hospital to Promote Prevention and Safe Housing
EPA, HHS, and HUD Regional Administrators Visit St. Christopher’s Hospital for Children to Highlight Lead Poisoning Prevention, Testing, and Safe Housing
PHILADELPHIA - Regional Administrators from U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), and U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) visited St. Christopher’s Hospital for Children in Philadelphia today to underscore a shared commitment to protecting children from lead exposure.
The visit highlighted the importance of public education, housing remediation, clinical screening, and safe drinking water as part of a coordinated federal effort to help families identify and reduce lead risks in their homes and immediate surroundings. Under the message “Get the Facts and Get Your Home Tested,” the agencies emphasized that parents and caregivers can take practical steps to protect children from lead in paint, dust, soil, and drinking water.
“Every child deserves to grow up in a safe environment, free from the preventable harms of lead exposure,” said EPA Mid-Atlantic Regional Administrator Amy Van Blarcom-Lackey. “At EPA, we are focused on the facts: replacing lead service lines, supporting clean and safe drinking water, and giving families the tools they need to understand and reduce risks in their homes. This is about protecting children today and preventing harm for generations to come.”
The visit also highlighted the role of federal investment in addressing legacy infrastructure and older housing stock, especially in communities that have historically faced higher environmental and health burdens. EPA is working with local and state partners to replace lead service lines and support clean drinking water in schools, childcare facilities, and residential systems across the region.
“Childhood lead poisoning is a public health issue that we can and must prevent,” said HHS Regional Director Tatiana Villa. “Clinical screening, family education, and early intervention are critical pieces of the solution. By working with EPA and HUD, we can better connect families to the information and resources they need to protect their children’s health.”
The agencies also stressed the importance of housing-related protections, including lead paint abatement and remediation in older homes, apartments, and public housing.
“Safe housing is a foundation for healthy families,” said Joseph DeFelice, HUD Assistant Deputy Secretary for Field Policy and Management and Region III Administrator. “HUD is committed to working with our federal partners and local leaders to reduce lead hazards in homes and neighborhoods, especially in communities with older housing stock. Collaboration is essential if we want to make real progress and ensure that every child has a chance to thrive.”
Together, the agencies are aligning environmental protection, housing mitigation, and health screening to address childhood lead poisoning from multiple angles. The joint visit underscored the power of interagency collaboration and the importance of focusing federal attention and resources on communities where children may face elevated risks.
The visit at St. Christopher’s Hospital for Children reflected a shared federal commitment to protecting children’s health, supporting community education, and ensuring that families have access to actionable tools and trusted information.
“At St. Christopher’s, keeping children healthy has been our mission for more than 150 years. When we help families prevent lead exposure, we are protecting children's ability to learn, grow, and reach their full potential. We are proud to stand alongside our community and public health partners in this important effort to keep kids safe,” said Claire Alminde, President, St. Christopher's Hospital for Children.
Families seeking to learn more about lead risks in their homes can:
- Get their home tested for lead hazards
- Check whether their drinking water service line may contain lead
- Talk with their health care provider about lead screening for children
- Use federal, state, and local resources to reduce exposure risks

Ranking Member Scott Slams ED for Playing Games with Public Service Loan Forgiveness Program
WASHINGTON – Today, House Education and Workforce Ranking Member Robert C. “Bobby” Scott (VA-03) demanded answers from Department of Education (ED) Secretary Linda McMahon, following concerning reports from borrowers in the Public Service Loan Forgiveness (PSLF) program that several qualifying payments were erased from their accounts.
Established in 2007, PSLF offers loan forgiveness to public servants who work for a qualified employer for 10 years and make 120 payments toward their federal student loans. However, borrowers have recently reported that the number of PSLF-qualifying payments, tracked on a counter on the Office for Federal Student Aid’s (FSA’s) website, appeared incorrect. Despite acknowledging the data error, ED failed to provide detailed information on the cause of the error.
“Without additional information from the Department, borrowers cannot know whether changes to the PSLF qualifying payment count were the result of an error that will be fixed; if it is a decision that can be appealed; or if the statement reflects an unappealable decision made by this Administration. Without any additional information, borrowers are left in the dark as to why they must remain in repayment longer than the law requires. This is particularly concerning if a borrower believes they have met all the statutory and regulatory requirements to have their debt forgiven through the PSLF,” wrote Ranking Member Scott.
In his letter, Ranking Member Scott also emphasized that the qualifying payment-count errors come as the Department has not addressed the 88,000-application backlog in the PSLF buyback program and has eliminated affordable repayment plans, creating financial uncertainty and distress for student loan borrowers.
On Friday, October 30, 2026, the American Federation of Teachers (AFT), with support from Protect Borrowers, sued the Trump Administration, alleging it unlawfully blocked student loan forgiveness for tens of thousands of borrowers who qualify. The lawsuit, Weingarten v. McMahon, alleges ED Secretary McMahon mismanaged PSLF by incorrectly counting borrowers’ payment timelines and not awarding people credit for time served.

Reps Peters, Vargas, Levin, and Jacobs Back San Diego County Registrar of Voters Amid Trump Admin Probe for Voter Data
November 2, 2026 
San Diego, CA — Today, U.S. Representative Scott Peters (CA-50) led members of the San Diego Congressional delegation, Reps. Juan Vargas (CA-52), Mike Levin (CA-49), and Sara Jacobs (CA-51), in a letter to U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche amid the Department of Justice’s (DOJ) attempt to sanction voter rolls across California, including in San Diego County’s Registrars of Voters (ROV). 
The DOJ demanded that San Diego’s ROV provide voter information for over 1,700 voters, including driver’s license numbers, Social Security numbers, and voter registration applications, within 48 hours, and withhold their ballots until their citizenship is confirmed. In its response, the County pushed back against several unsubstantiated claims and argued that the DOJ's probe violated several election laws. 
The Members' letter reinforced the County’s claims and acknowledged that California’s registrars follow all state and federal election laws, including citizenship attestation and database verification through the California Secretary of State. They argued that the DOJ’s letter cites no legal authority to direct county ballot administration and that it violates the National Voter Registration Act’s (NVRA) 90-day quiet period against systematically removing voters from the rolls. 
“The information requested by DOJ is intended to confirm the department’s unsubstantiated allegations of noncitizen voting in California,” the Members noted, also pointing to the data cited by DOJ, which the Agency itself conceded “may be outdated or incomplete.” 
The Members also stated that unverified fraud allegations do not give registrars authority to violate federal law by refusing to count the votes of people already deemed eligible. They added that the DOJ’s demand fails to explain who would determine citizenship status, how, or when, less than a week before Election Day. 
“The request from DOJ violates the NVRA, Voting Rights Act, California state law, and jeopardizes Californians’ constitutional right to vote,” the Members concluded, adding that “as Members of the California Congressional delegation, we commend the work of our state ROVs to ensure state and federal election laws are upheld.” 
Background: Over the past several weeks, the DOJ has escalated pressure on California before Election Day and made unsubstantiated claims that large numbers of illegal voters are on the rolls. Federal courts have repeatedly intervened and denied the Administration’s attempt to interfere. 
In May, California Attorney General Rob Bonta joined Rep. Peters’ podcast, 72 and Sunny, to debunk the myth of widespread voter fraud, discuss how California has pushed back against the attacks from the Trump Administration, and highlight how the State is enhancing voter security for the election. Watch the full episode here.

OPM Announces Opening of Applications for 2027–2028 White House Fellows Program
WASHINGTON, DC — The US Office of Personnel Management (OPM) today announced that applications are now open for the 2027–2028 class of White House Fellows, offering exceptional Americans a unique opportunity to serve at the highest levels of the federal government and help shape the future of our nation.
Established in 1964, the White House Fellows Program is one of the nation’s most prestigious leadership and public service programs. Each year, a select group of accomplished individuals from across the country is chosen to spend a year working alongside cabinet secretaries, senior White House staff, and other top government officials, gaining firsthand experience in federal leadership and policymaking.
“The White House Fellows Program represents an extraordinary opportunity for talented Americans to bring their experience, ideas, and leadership to public service,” OPM Director Scott Kupor said. “Some of our nation’s most accomplished leaders got their start as White House Fellows, and we want the next generation of innovators, problem-solvers, and public servants to see what they can contribute. If you’ve ever considered serving your country, this is an opportunity to step forward, make a meaningful impact, and help shape the future of government.”
"This program has a distinguished legacy of leadership and public service that reaches back more than six decades,” Executive Director of the President's Commission on White House Fellows Mary Sprowls said. “We encourage patriotic, highly-motivated, and exceptional Americans to consider applying or urge others to apply.”
Selected Fellows participate in a full-time, paid fellowship in Washington, DC, where they work directly with senior administration officials on consequential issues facing the nation. In addition to their professional assignments, Fellows participate in an intensive education program featuring candid discussions with distinguished leaders from the public and private sectors, as well as community service initiatives that strengthen their commitment to civic engagement.
Since its founding, nearly 900 Americans have participated in the program, including Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Dan Caine, former Secretary of State General Colin Powell, former Secretary of Transportation Elaine Chao, Pulitzer Prize-winning historian Doris Kearns Goodwin, and US Senators Bill Hagerty and Dan Sullivan. White House Fellows alumni have gone on to serve as military leaders, educators, entrepreneurs, scientists, nonprofit founders, and executives, united by a shared commitment to serving their communities and country.
Applications for the 2027–2028 White House Fellows class are open now. Interested candidates can learn more about the program and application process here.
title: OPM Announces Opening of Applications for 2027–2028 White House Fellows Program

Colchester, Vt. – “At midnight it was time to move,” said retired U.S. Army Sgt. 1st Class Pete Ferrell, recalling a night in Afghanistan.
He gripped the handle of one of the four corners of a field stretcher carrying a wounded Soldier. A tray of medical equipment on the Soldier’s chest chirped as it monitored vital signs and sustained him. The team of four Soldiers locked step, carrying the patient onto a plane bound for a higher level of care.
As the plane transporting the wounded Soldier took off, Ferrell found himself on the same runway at Bagram Airfield where the deployment began months earlier. There at the feet of the towering Hindu Kush mountain range, four decades and nearly 3,000 miles stood between him and the jungles he hovered over in a UH-1 “Huey” helicopter in Vietnam, during his first combat tour.
In 2010, at age 62, Ferrell secured an age waiver and volunteered for the deployment to Afghanistan with the Vermont Army National Guard’s 86th Infantry Brigade Combat Team (Mountain).
“He always seeks something bigger than himself to be part of, that’s just who Pete is,” said U.S. Army Maj. Beth Carrier, a physician assistant with the New Hampshire Army National Guard who deployed with Ferrell to Bosnia in 1999 when she was a flight medic. “I can only hope that somewhere in my life that I am a fraction as good of a human as he is.”
For many, it’s hard to imagine that the Vietnam veteran who flew over 250 combat hours as a Huey crew chief and survived being shot down in Laos felt he owed more.
“I never got wounded or had PTSD. I was still capable, and I felt I still had to do more,” said Ferrell.
When he arrived in Da Nang, Vietnam, in 1970 as a helicopter mechanic, he was assigned to the night maintenance shift in a hangar. It was far from the excitement of flying he had imagined as a child in Braintree, Massachusetts, watching planes take off and land at the airport and flying his own model aircraft.
So, he went to his platoon sergeant and asked for a flight platoon assignment. A few days later, the platoon sergeant told him to shadow another Soldier who showed him how to do daily maintenance on a Huey.
“Then he says, ‘OK that one’s yours,’” said Ferrell.
From then on, the 22-year-old specialist was now in charge of his own helicopter.
“We learned a lot about maintenance in training, but overseeing a whole aircraft was a lot of responsibility.”
But along with the added responsibility, he also got his childhood wish.
“When the aircraft flew, you went with it,” he said.
Ferrell said he mostly flew “ash and trash missions” – lift missions that could include transporting anything from troops to supplies to mail.
However, about three months before his tour ended, his unit was selected for Operation Lam 719, a highly contested two-month offensive where they flew South Vietnamese troops into southeastern Laos. The objective was to disrupt North Vietnam’s military supply network on the Ho Chi Minh Trail.
Ferrell said he knew this mission was not routine; the danger felt so imminent that he prayed.
“I started out saying the 23rd Psalm when we took off on the first three sorties, and by the fourth one I must have gotten too comfortable,” he said. “One pilot said to the other, ‘Stay tight to this hill,’ and he no sooner said that and the windshield for the aircraft was blown out.”
The aircraft crashed, but Ferrell and the rest of the crew survived.
“Somebody started yelling, ‘Come on, come on!’” he said, adding that another aircraft had landed nearby and they all started running to it. “I grabbed my M16 and started tromping through the jungle, and we all got on the other aircraft and flew out.”
It wasn’t until Ferrell was on the plane flying home from Vietnam with a ream of military records that he realized he had received 10 Air Medals for his combat flight hours, one with a valor device for the mission on which he was shot down.
He finished his active-duty service in 1973 and settled into civilian life. He married Deb, the woman he exchanged letters with throughout the war, and moved to Vermont where they had their first son.
Then in 1981 he heard a familiar sound and looked up in the Vermont sky and saw Hueys overhead. Ferrell said he knew he had to track them down. He found them in a hangar in Burlington, Vermont, at a Vermont Army Guard aviation unit.
“I walked in and there were 12 Hueys there and it was like a homecoming. I was home again,” he said.
Ferrell met with a flight platoon sergeant who assuaged his fears that if he joined the Guard he might end up sweeping floors rather than maintaining and flying aircraft.
And with that, Ferrell re-enlisted and was back working on Hueys.
In 1998, the unit transitioned to the UH-60 Black Hawk helicopter and assumed a medevac mission. Ferrell was hesitant about learning a new aircraft and mission. That was until he teamed up with Carrier, then a 20-year-old specialist so passionate about her role as a flight medic that she inspired him.
“She taught me that it was all about saving lives, and there’s no better mission than that,” he said.
Ferrell didn’t come around right away, though, Carrier said, adding he refused to do medical training and insisted his job as the crew chief didn’t require it. However, he changed his tune after they medevaced a Soldier with severe appendicitis – their first real-world patient in Bosnia.
After the mission, Ferrell told Carrier that her ability to help the Soldier had captivated him, but he admitted he felt helpless to assist.
“He completely did a 180 on the entire idea of not touching a patient. It was a 100% adjustment of his thought process,” she said. “From then on, he wanted to do all he could, asking ‘What can I do? What can I learn? What can you teach me so I can help you?’”
In turn, he used his knowledge of the aircraft to help her set her medical gear up to deliver care more expediently. These were lessons she would take with her when their careers parted ways, and she deployed to Iraq and later when she was commissioned as an officer and went on to study medicine.
But the two remained close. Ferrell was even the “man of honor” at her wedding, which required him to don a raspberry pink shirt for the occasion.
“I always knew with him I was well protected. On the hoist he could drop me on a dime. I always knew that the aircraft that we were on was the safest that it could possibly be. That was because of Pete's work ethic,” she said.
When Ferrell returned from the Bosnia deployment, personnel moves in the aviation unit led him to move on from aviation. Eventually, he was assigned to the headquarters of the 86th IBCT (MTN), which led to his Afghanistan deployment.
When Ferrell told his wife and sons about volunteering for the deployment, he said they were the only people in his family who didn’t think he was crazy.
“It’s just a part of who he is, and it’s how they [his sons] always knew their father,” said his wife. “So, it was just, he’s going to be gone for a while, but he’ll be back and we will, as we say, improvise, adapt and overcome.”
When he arrived in Afghanistan, his daily duties at the headquarters company kept him mostly at Bagram, but as he had throughout his career, Ferrell felt he still had more to give.
One night he stumbled upon it while sitting in the base’s operations center. A major from another section told him he had a mission at the airfield. Ferrell’s interest was piqued. It turned out that the officer had inadvertently found Ferrell another medevac mission; transferring wounded patients from the field hospital onto aircraft bound to take them to facilities with higher levels of care.
“You know like Beth had taught me, saving lives is the greatest mission there is, and that is what it was,” he said.
He began to stop at the hospital every day after his shift to ask if volunteers were needed that night but never mentioned his side quests to anybody in his unit until years later. He continued the late-night missions until he returned home from Afghanistan just before Christmas 2010.
By then, he was 63 years old, three years past the standard mandatory retirement age, and finally retired from the military in 2011 with 33 years of service.
“You get home from Vietnam, you realize how many men were lost and how many were wounded, and you think, ‘Why me? Why did I survive?’” he said. “You figure out that there is a plan here, so you have to go with it. You take it as the blessing that you were saved for a reason. I can look back now and say that this is where God was pointing me.”
title: From Vietnam to Afghanistan: A Vermont Guard member’s lifetime of service

Press Statement

Marco Rubio, Secretary of State

November 2, 2026

On behalf of the United States of America, I extend warm congratulations to the people and government of Antigua and Barbuda on the 45th anniversary of your independence.

The United States and Antigua and Barbuda share a longstanding friendship grounded in our common democratic values, strong people-to-people ties, and commitment to a safe, secure, and prosperous Caribbean. Since establishing diplomatic relations in 1981, our two countries have worked together on issues ranging from regional security and law enforcement to economic development, and disaster preparedness.

We value Antigua and Barbuda’s partnership in advancing security and stability throughout the Eastern Caribbean and look forward to continuing our close cooperation on issues of mutual importance. As you mark this milestone, I wish you all a happy 45th Independence Day.

Lt. Gen. Philip Garrant, Space Systems Command commander, Lt. Gen. Gregory Gagnon, Combat Forces Command commander, and Maj. Gen. James Smith, Space Training and Readiness Command commander, each delivered a keynote address reinforcing the messages of readiness, speed and industry partnership to standing-room-only audiences in town to learn about mission area priorities.
Performing while transforming
“My message is straightforward,” Garrant said. “We are changing how we work: how we connect with operators and mission partners; how we work with industry; and how we equip our workforce to move at the pace the mission demands.”
Garrant listed numerous changes across Space Systems Command in the past year regarding capability, space industry connections and workforce improvements. SSC delivered the final GPS III satellite to orbit in a year that saw a historic launch pace from both coasts. The Victus Haze launch demonstrated that the command could launch within 16 hours from notice to launch and get capability on orbit quickly.
Driving the U.S. Space Force’s Commercial Space Strategy is SSC’s Commercial Space Office (COMSO), which announced that its new Enterprise Space Activity Group (ESAG) and Working Capital Fund executed $1.2 billion across 162 contracts for commercial SATCOM operational capability. COMSO also announced the launch of its new Access to the Classified Ecosystem for Space (ACES), designed to enable better industry participation in war games, exercises and classified events through COMSO-assisted security clearances for companies with a U.S. Department of War sponsor.
Garrant also shared industry feedback demonstrating the command’s progress in hitting small business goals, as well as commercial access, pathways and contract awards, while realistically acknowledging areas where improvements remain underway when it comes to clarity, follow-through and conversion to mission outcomes.
“Next October, we will be right back here at Space Industry Days to show you our work again,” Garrant said. “That is our commitment: continue delivering today’s mission, continue transforming for tomorrow’s fight, and continue being candid about both.”
“What’s going to happen in 15 years?”
In his Oct. 22 keynote, Gagnon began by outlining how the three commands work together.
“In Combat Forces Command, it’s our job to take the people and the kit and turn it into combat-credible, ready-to-fight, ready-to-win forces,” Gagnon explained. “We also have to build the tactics, techniques, procedures and coordinate functions inside the joint force so that spacepower can fuel our ability as a nation, not just to defend ourselves, but to power project.”
Gagnon said there are a lot of things the U.S. Space Force has done right. CFC has operationally accepted more than 50 different capabilities this year, as well as cyber-hardened both weapons systems and installations. He noted that the 16-hour Victus Nox launch, which demonstrated the U.S. Space Force’s ability to rapidly launch and get capability on orbit, “didn’t exist 24 to 36 months ago.”
In 2011, the U.S. Space Force had 18 launches. This year, it is projecting more than 170 — a more than eightfold increase powered by reusable commercial launch. In 2011, one launch equaled about 1.5 satellites in space; today, a single launch can put 50 satellites on orbit.
“Combat realities change quickly,” Gagnon said. “Militaries that adapt, win.”
“We are changing, not just to change,” Gagnon said. “We are changing because we are facing a very aggressive, fast-moving adversary. We are moving fast because we’re in a race and in this race, second place loses.”
CFC has learned several things from major combat operations, Gagnon said. Mobility equals survivability, and it’s not just the ability to “box it up and move,” but the ability to do so repeatedly, Gagnon said. Camouflage, concealment and deception are in vogue again.
“We need to plan and budget for the fact that we will have attrition,” Gagnon said. “Our operations units have just enough equipment to do their job. You need three times the amount of equipment to do your job when you start planning for attrition.”
“What we do, not everyone can do,” Gagnon said. “And I will tell you, our greatest advantage over other militaries is our people. Our people want to be in the military, they volunteered, and they’re highly educated compared to our potential adversaries. U.S. enlisted forces, whether it’s in the maritime services, the space service or the Army, do functions that in foreign militaries are only done by officers. Our people are the special sauce.”
What happens the day after a capability is delivered to the joint force?
Smith explained in his keynote address, “STARCOM’s responsibility begins where a program milestone alone cannot answer the most important question: What happens the day after delivery?”
“Think about everything that’s gone into that moment,” Smith said. “Engineers have solved difficult technical problems, teams have worked requirements and design reviews, and people have made hard choices about costs and schedule. A new capability has reached the force.”
“That is a significant accomplishment, but put yourself in the position of the Guardian who has to use it,” Smith said. “That Guardian needs to understand what the system can do, what its limitations are and how to employ it as part of a larger mission. The force needs tactics to account for those limitations. Commanders need evidence about how the capability will perform under the conditions they expect to face.”
“That’s where the distance between capability, delivery and combat credibility becomes visible,” Smith explained. “STARCOM helps close the distance by developing Guardians, evaluating capabilities and bringing people and systems together with the tactics they need to succeed. Our contribution gives the force a stronger foundation for operational employment.”
“Industry partnership belongs in that work from the beginning,” Smith said. “The choices made during development affect what an instructor can teach, and what a tester can observe. They affect how a capability connects to another system and how quickly supporting training can change. We earn combat credibility by understanding how Guardians, systems and tactics perform together.”
Smith shared how industry can help by designing for trainability so that Guardians can practice the capability they actually operate. Give test teams the data, instrumentation, models and access required to allow Guardians to understand performance under realistic conditions. Industry also can help by designing for integration and adaptation. Interfaces need to be usable across the mission thread, and industry can build technical and business approaches that support meaningful updates at operational speed. Finally, Smith said, industry should stay engaged after the first delivery.
“These are concrete areas where industry can contribute,” Smith said. “Bring us an explanation of the mission problem your approach addresses, and the work it enables. Everyone must be equally clear about the requirements and the evidence we need. That is how industry helps us all forge a combat-credible Space Force.”
title: USSF field command leaders appeal to commercial space industry at Space Industry Days

text:
Congressman Vicente Gonzalez Delivers $800,000 for Safer Streets, Improved Trauma Response to Roadway Crashes
Contact: Alexis Torres
Washington, D.C. – Today, Congressman Vicente Gonzalez (TX-34) announced $800,000 in federal funding for the Rio Grande Valley Regional Advisory Council on Trauma, Service Area V to save lives by reducing the risk of serious injuries on roadways across Cameron, Willacy, Hidalgo and Starr Counties. The funds, allocated through the U.S. Department of Transportation’s (DOT) Safe Streets and Roads for All program, will be used to develop a Comprehensive Safety Action Plan focused on post-crash care and to conduct training at Regional Medical Operations Centers. This work will include regional coordination planning, performance analysis, and piloting real-time trauma resource and prehospital whole blood monitoring technology to improve EMS routing, resource visibility, and survivability.
“Safer streets require stronger investments in our communities. Today’s announcement gives our trauma centers additional resources and support to deliver the best possible care in life-or-death situations where every second matters,” said Congressman Gonzalez. “Since being elected to Congress, I have brought down nearly $8 billion in federal funding to our region, and I will continue working with our federal and local partners to build on these investments to create a better future for South Texas families.
Today’s announcement was made possible by Congressman Gonzalez’s support of the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, which was enacted in 2021, and authorized $5 billion in appropriated funds over five years (2022-2026) to prevent roadway fatalities and serious injury. The Rio Grande Valley Trauma Regional Advisory Council is committed to improving specialized healthcare to South Texans through education, outreach, collaboration and communication. Trauma Service Area V consists of the four counties, Cameron, Willacy, Hidalgo and Starr, located at the southernmost tip of Texas. There are 13 hospitals in the region and 12 of which serve as trauma-designated facilities.
title: Congressman Vicente Gonzalez Delivers $800,000 for Safer Streets, Improved Trauma Response to Roadway Crashes

William Rondell Lashawn Smith, 44, from Fort Dodge and Des Moines, Iowa, but most recently living in Johnston, Iowa, was sentenced on October 30, 2026, in federal court in Sioux City to 152 months’ imprisonment. Smith pled guilty on April 21, 2026, to one count of conspiracy to distribute methamphetamine, three counts of distribution of methamphetamine and one count of possession with intent to distribute methamphetamine.

Evidence at the plea and sentencing hearings showed that from January 2023 through February 2024, Smith was involved in a conspiracy that distributed more than 14 kilograms of methamphetamine in the Fort Dodge, Iowa area. On three occasions in February 2024, Smith distributed over 2 ½ pounds of methamphetamine to an individual cooperating with law enforcement. On one of those occasions, the distribution occurred within 1,000 feet of Meriwether Park in Fort Dodge. In February 2024, officers searched two of Smith’s properties and seized cocaine, methamphetamine, over $8,000, three firearms, and drug distribution materials, including two scales.

United States District Court Judge Leonard T. Strand sentenced Smith to 152 months’ imprisonment and a ten-year term of supervised release. There is no parole in the federal system. Smith is currently in the custody of U.S. Marshals until he can be transported to a federal prison.

The case was prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney Shawn S. Wehde and was investigated by Iowa Division of Narcotics Enforcement, Iowa DCI Laboratory, Fort Dodge Police Department, Webster County Sheriff’s Office, Iowa State Patrol, and Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives.

Court file information at https://ecf.iand.uscourts.gov/cgi-bin/login.pl .

The case file number is 25-3005. Follow us on X @USAO_NDIA.

WASHINGTON – Savon Lee Blanchard, 33, a previously convicted killer residing in Temple Hills, Maryland, pleaded guilty today in U.S. District Court in connection with his illegal possession of a Glock 30 pistol that was recovered following a foot chase after police stopped him on a stolen ATV, announced U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro.

Blanchard pleaded guilty before Judge Sparkle L. Sooknanan to one count of unlawful possession of a firearm by a convicted felon. Judge Sooknanan scheduled sentencing for March 2, 2027.

Blanchard was previously convicted in 2016 in Prince Georges County of involuntary manslaughter in the 2011 fatal shooting of 23-year-old Alusine Kargbo of Lanham, who was shot in the back as he played basketball at an elementary school in New Carrollton. For that slaying, Blanchard was sentenced to 10 years in prison with five years suspended for the murder and sentenced to an additional 20 years in prison for use of a handgun in commission of a crime of violence for which he was sentenced to 20 years in prison with 15 years suspended.

According to court documents, on April 17, 2026, about 5:20 p.m., Blanchard was sitting on a white Yamaha Raptor 700R 4-wheeler, an All-Terrain Vehicle (ATV), that was stopped and running near the intersection of Nannie Helen Burroughs Avenue NE and Hayes Street NE. At the same time, Metropolitan Police officers and agents from the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives drove by on patrol.

The stolen Yamaha Raptor ATV.

An MPD investigator attempted to initiate a traffic stop of the ATV and pulled his marked patrol vehicle in front of the ATV to stop it from fleeing. An ATF agent pulled his own patrol vehicle directly behind the ATV.

Blanchard (circled in red) flees from law enforcement. The Glock is circled in yellow.

Blanchard dismounted the ATV and fled on foot. Law enforcement chased Blanchard down the sidewalk. As officers ran, they heard a metal object clank against the sidewalk. One of the agents stopped and recovered a black Glock Model 30 .45 caliber pistol that Blanchard had dropped. The firearm was loaded with 12 rounds in the magazine. Another round was found on the ground near the weapon.

Police recovered this Glock Model 30 and a magazine containing 12 rounds.

Police and ATF agents apprehended Blanchard moments later. A check on the ATV revealed it had been reported stolen out of Anne Arundel County. Subsequently, officers reviewed footage from surveillance cameras that showed them chasing Blanchard, the Glock coming off Blanchard’s person as he ran, and the Glock sliding along the concrete sidewalk.

As a previously convicted felon, Blanchard was prohibited from carrying any firearm.

This case was investigated by the Metropolitan Police Department and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, Washington Field Office. The matter is being prosecuted under the Make D.C. Safe and Beautiful initiative by Assistant U.S. Attorney Emory V. Cole. Make D.C. Safe and Beautiful is a law enforcement initiative in support of President Trump’s Executive Order to crack down on gun violence, prioritize federal firearms violations, pursue tougher penalties, and seek detention for federal firearms violators.

CHARLESTON, W.Va. – Willie Davis McCall III, also known as “Primo” and “Ill Will,” 43, of Warren, Michigan, was sentenced today to 12 years in prison, to be followed by 10 years of supervised release, for distribution of 40 grams or more of fentanyl.

According to court documents and statements made in court, on April 30, 2025, McCall sold approximately 55.53 grams of a substance containing fentanyl to a confidential informant in exchange for $2,700. As part of his guilty plea, McCall admitted that he conducted the transaction while in a parked vehicle in Charleston.

McCall further admitted that he distributed or possessed with the intent to distribute nearly 500 grams of fentanyl from in or about April 2025 through in or about June 2025. The distributions included the sale of approximately 55.40 grams of fentanyl on April 3, 2025, and of approximately 55.57 grams of fentanyl on June 11, 2025, each time to a confidential informant in Charleston in exchange for $2,700.

On June 17, 2025, law enforcement officers executed a search warrant at the Charleston residence where McCall was living and seized from his bedroom closet approximately 322.16 grams of fentanyl found in six bags and $5,557. McCall admitted that he planned to distribute the seized fentanyl in and around the Southern District of West Virginia, and that the seized cash was drug proceeds.

The Court sentenced McCall as a career offender. As part of his guilty plea, McCall admitted that he was previously convicted of distribution of methamphetamine in United States District Court for the Southern District of West Virginia on July 26, 2017, a serious drug offense for which he was sentenced to more than one year in prison. McCall’s criminal history also includes multiple prior convictions in Michigan and Ohio for offenses including carjacking, assault with intent to murder, possession of a firearm during commission of a felony offense, possession of a firearm by a prohibited person, and domestic violence.

"Career drug traffickers who continue to distribute fentanyl despite prior convictions should expect to face serious consequences,” said United States Attorney Moore Capito. “This defendant repeatedly violated the law and contributed to the flow of a highly lethal substance into our communities. We remain committed to aggressively prosecuting fentanyl dealers and seeking significant penalties for those who endanger public safety through the distribution of this deadly drug."

Capito made the announcement and commended the investigative work of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) and the Charleston Police Department.

United States District Judge Joseph R. Goodwin imposed the sentence. Assistant United States Attorney Lesley C. Shamblin prosecuted the case.

This case is part of Operation Take Back America , a nationwide initiative that marshals the full resources of the Department of Justice to repel the invasion of illegal immigration, achieve the total elimination of cartels and transnational criminal organizations (TCOs), and protect our communities from the perpetrators of violent crime.

This case is also part of Project Safe Neighborhoods (PSN), the Department of Justice’s nationwide initiative that brings federal, state, local, and tribal law enforcement, prosecutors, and other public safety partners together to coordinate efforts to combat violent crime and make communities safe. Coordinated by U.S. Attorneys’ offices in each of the 94 federal districts, PSN is tailored to particular communities to strategically address specific violent crime and public safety challenges. As a key component of Operation Take Back America, PSN serves a central role in the Department’s commitment to make our country safe. PSN emphasizes three core principles: rapid federal response to violent crime and criminal offenders; strong, strategic partnerships among law enforcement at all levels; and accountability and deterrence through the prosecution of the most serious, readily provable offenses and other strategies. These efforts complement and strengthen President Trump’s Homeland Security Task Forces, ensuring a comprehensive federal response to the most pressing public safety issues facing communities.

A copy of this press release is located on the website of the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of West Virginia. Related court documents and information can be found on PACER by searching for Case No. 2:25-cr-192.
title: Michigan Man Sentenced to 12 Years in Prison for Fentanyl Crime

LOS ANGELES – Six additional foreign nationals residing in the Antelope and San Fernando valleys of Los Angeles County have been charged in federal criminal complaints alleging they illegally registered to vote and voted in California then lied about it on their forms to become naturalized United States citizens, the Justice Department announced today.

The following six additional defendants are charged with making false statements on their naturalization applications:

Sirgalahad Camua, 43, a citizen of the Philippines who resides in Palmdale;

Krystel Capi Valle, 31, a Mexican national living in Palmdale;

Moria Dahan, 35, an Israeli national living in West Hills;

Chad Goertz, 52, a Canadian citizen living in Agua Dulce;

Mahyar Nikzad, 35, an Iranian national living in Canoga Park; and

Gilberto Ruiz, 46, a citizen of Mexico who resides in Palmdale.

These additional criminal charges are a part of “Operation Protect the Vote” – an ongoing, coordinated federal effort in California to root out fraud in U.S. elections and protect electoral integrity.

“Today, my office announces criminal charges against six additional noncitizens for unlawfully registering and voting in our elections,” said First Assistant United States Attorney Bill Essayli. “We have now charged 34 defendants in Operation Protect the Vote, and every one of their names was on the list we provided to California officials. There are thousands of suspected noncitizens on California’s voter rolls, and we renew our request for California to expeditiously work with us to verify the citizenship of those casting ballots in elections. Every illegal vote cast and counted cancels the legitimate vote of an American citizen. We will continue to arrest and prosecute those who threaten our democratic republic through unlawful vote dilution.”

“We must protect the vote of every American citizen,” said Erin Burke, Special Agent in Charge of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) Los Angeles. “HSI will follow the evidence wherever it leads and work to hold accountable those who violate federal law. We thank the U.S. Attorney's Office for its leadership and partnership.”

“Protecting the integrity of our elections is not a Republican or Democratic issue – it is an American and Californian responsibility,” said San Luis Obispo County District Attorney Dan Dow. “We appreciate our federal partners’ assistance and will independently investigate every credible allegation of illegal voting, follow the evidence, and enforce California law while safeguarding the rights of every accused person.”

Every defendant charged in Operation Protect the Vote is a lawful permanent resident (LPR) or commonly known as having a “green card.” LPRs are not U.S. citizens and are not legally permitted to register to vote or to vote in U.S. elections.

The defendants arrested today – Camua, Capi Valle, Dahan, Goertz, and Nikzad – are scheduled to make their initial appearances this afternoon in U.S. District Court in Los Angeles.

According to affidavits filed with the complaints, Camua illegally registered to vote in August 2009 by falsely claiming to be a U.S. citizen. He voted by mail-in ballot in May 2020, November 2024, and June 2026. In May 2025, Camua filed paperwork seeking to become a naturalized U.S. citizen and, under penalty of perjury, falsely stated that he had neither claimed to be a U.S. citizen nor had he registered to vote in U.S. elections.

Capi Valle in June 2026 swore under penalty of perjury on her naturalization form that she had never claimed to be a U.S. citizen nor had she registered to vote in U.S. elections. In fact, in October 2022 she illegally registered to vote by lying that she was a U.S. citizen. She then illegally voted by mail-in ballot in the November 2022 election.

Dahan illegally registered to vote and voted in person on November 5, 2024, the date of the U.S. general election. She falsely claimed under penalty of perjury to be a U.S. citizen. On her naturalization form dated November 6, 2025, she falsely stated under penalty of perjury that she never claimed to be a U.S. citizen nor had she registered to vote in a U.S. election.

Goertz illegally registered to vote in April 2018 and illegally voted by mail in the November 2022 and November 2024 U.S. elections. In February 2026, Goertz lied under oath on his naturalization form when he denied having ever claimed to be a U.S. citizen and denied having ever registered to vote in a U.S. election.

In September 2024, Nikzad illegally registered to voted and under penalty of perjury checked the box on his voter registration form reading, “I am a U.S. citizen.” Records indicate that Nikzad voted in the March 2024 and November 2024 U.S. elections. In February 2026, under penalty of perjury, he falsely stated that he never claimed to be a U.S. citizen and denied ever registering to become a U.S. voter.

Ruiz in July 2022 registered to vote and he voted by mail-in ballot in three elections: November 2022, March 2024, and November 2024, falsely claiming to be a U.S. citizen. In August 2025, under penalty of perjury, Ruiz denied ever claiming to be a U.S. citizen and denied having ever registered to vote.

A criminal complaint merely contains allegations. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

If convicted, each defendant would face a statutory maximum sentence of five years in federal prison.

Homeland Security Investigations is investigating these matters.

Assistant United States Attorneys Michael Wheat and Minjae Kim of the Orange County Office are prosecuting these cases.
title: Six Additional Foreign Nationals in L.A. County Who Registered to Vote and Voted in U.S. Elections Charged with Lying on Naturalization Forms

Orlando, Florida – Thirteen foreign nationals from Brazil and Cuba have been charged by indictment for their roles in a conspiracy to defraud the United States and other aliens. The charges include conspiracy to commit wire fraud, wire fraud, visa fraud, unlawful employment of aliens, and marriage fraud. United States Attorney Gregory W. Kehoe made the announcement.

Vagner Sorares De Almeida (age 54), Juliana Colucci (age 47), Lucas Felipe Trindade Silva (age 34), and Ronaldo De Campos (age 35) are each charged with one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud and two counts of wire fraud. They are also charged with four counts of conspiracy to commit visa fraud, one count of conspiracy to commit marriage fraud, and one count of unlawful employment of aliens.

Erick Bruno Goncalves De Assis Pinto (age 34), Nathalia Da Costa Ferreira (age 43), Nathalia Gomes Ciriaco (age 29), and Kelen Cristina Da Silva (age 37) are each charged with charged with one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud, two counts of wire fraud, and four counts of conspiracy to commit visa fraud.

Issac Antonio Narvaez (age 69) is charged with three counts of conspiracy to commit marriage fraud.

Ronay Castillo Salazar (age 51), Rebeca Aldama Garcia (age 40), Mijail Cabera Nunez (age 52), and Lorraine Soares Oliverira (age 32) are each charged with one count of conspiracy to commit marriage fraud.

According to court records, from August 18, 2023, through April 20, 2026, Vagner Sorares De Almeida owned and operated a corporate entity registered in Florida called Legacy Imigra Solutions LLC (“Legacy”). Juliana Colucci, Lucas Felipe Trindade Silva, Nathalia Da Costa Ferreira, Nathalia Gomes Ciriaco, Ronaldo De Campos, Erick Bruno Goncalves De Assis Pinto, and Kelen Cristina Da Silva were employees of the company. Legacy falsely purported to be a professional establishment employed by immigration experts and attorneys who could assist individuals with immigration-related legal work. It was part of the conspiracy to give false, inaccurate, and incomplete legal and immigration advice to prospective clients to induce them to retain Legacy’s services. Legacy would falsify immigration documents to fraudulently obtain immigration status and benefits for their clients. The defendants also engaged in a regular practice of hiring aliens knowing that the individuals were unauthorized for employment in the United States. Vagner Sorares De Almeida, Juliana Colucci, Ronay Castillo Salazar, Rebeca Aldama Garcia, Mijail Cabera Nunez, Lorraine Soares Oliverira, and Issac Antonio Narvaez also conspired to commit marriage fraud.

If convicted, each count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud and wire fraud carries a maximum penalty of 20 years’ imprisonment. The conspiracy to commit visa fraud offenses are each punishable up to 10 years’ imprisonment. The maximum penalty for conspiracy to commit marriage fraud is 5 years in federal prison, and unlawful employment of aliens carries a maximum penalty of 6 months’ imprisonment.

An indictment is merely a formal charge that a defendant has committed one or more violations of federal criminal law, and every defendant is presumed innocent unless, and until, proven guilty.

This case is being investigated by the Homeland Security Investigations (Orlando, Tampa, and Brasilia), the Internal Revenue Service Criminal Investigation, the United States Department of Labor Office of Inspector General, United States Department of Agriculture Office of Inspector General, United States Citizenship and Immigration Services, U.S. Customs and Border Protection, United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s Enforcement and Removal Operations, the United States Marshals Service, the Orange County Sheriff’s Office, Florida Highway Patrol and the Florida Department of Law Enforcement. It is being prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney Bianca Bansal.

This case is part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of United States law enforcement towards identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States. HSTF Region 20 comprises agents and officers from multiple law enforcement agencies with the prosecution being led by the United States Attorney’s Office for the Middle District of Florida.

The Department of War's Office of Strategic Capital (OSC) announced today a conditional loan commitment of up to $450 million to Neros, Inc., a U.S.-based developer and manufacturer of dual-use small unmanned aircraft systems (sUAS).
This investment is intended to support Neros' domestic manufacturing expansion and reduce reliance on foreign-made components.
OSC's conditional loan commitment to Neros directly advances President Donald J. Trump's Executive Order 14307, Unleashing American Drone Dominance. OSC financing alongside additional private capital will support Neros' planned expansion of vertically integrated domestic manufacturing capacity to produce dual-use sUAS platforms, ground control systems, and critical components like motors, radios, flight electronics, sensors, and batteries.
"Neros has already demonstrated an ability to design, manufacture, and deliver exceptional small unmanned aircraft systems," said David A. Lorch, Director of the Office of Strategic Capital and Senior Advisor to Deputy Secretary of War Steve Feinberg. "OSC's investment will turbocharge Neros' ability to manufacture drones and components critical for the production of drone systems."
Neros designs and produces low-cost, high-performance drones. The company's manufacturing facility in Torrance, California will help onshore the production of complete drone systems as well as critical subcomponents including propulsion motors, flight stacks, radios, and thermal sensors. This vertically integrated capacity will support both Neros' internal production and the supply of critical, NDAA-compliant components to other U.S. and allied drone manufacturers.
"Winning the drone industrial-base competition requires the United States to be able to manufacture complete systems at scale and at competitive prices for both military and non-military applications. This starts with bolstering the domestic supply of critical components inside all drone systems," said James R. Shanahan, Senior Managing Director (Investments) at OSC. "Neros' vertically integrated approach would support the creation of significant incremental domestic component capacity for Neros and the broader unmanned-systems ecosystem."
The conditional loan commitment specifies additional steps Neros must complete before financial close, including satisfying various financial, legal, technical, investment, due diligence and other requirements.
"I applaud OSC for helping to strengthen the domestic drone supply chain. Achieving Secretary Hegseth's mandate for American drone dominance requires a secure and resilient industrial base here at home," said Emil Michael, Under Secretary of War for Research and Engineering.
title: Department of War's Office of Strategic Capital Signs Conditional Loan Commitment of up to $450 Million With Neros, Inc.

Salinas, Bonamici, Merkley, Wyden Secure over $500,000 for Tualatin Soil and Water Conservation District
Tualatin, OR — Today, Congresswomen Andrea Salinas (OR-06) and Suzanne Bonamici (OR-01), alongside Oregon Senators Ron Wyden and Jeff Merkley, announced they secured the release of over $530,000 in federal funding from the Natural Resources Conservation Service (NRCS) to support Tualatin Soil and Water Conservation District (TSWCD).
In 2022, TSWCD applied to the NRCS for funding to improve fish habitat in Washington County. This work included replacing deteriorated culverts with bridges and modern culverts that help threatened species like steelhead trout move through local waterways. In February 2024, NRCS approved and obligated $1,074,887 to reimburse TSWCD for their work.
As of early September 2026, NRCS had only paid $543,837 of the over $1.07 million they had promised to TSWCD. This $531,000 shortfall has severely challenged TSWCD’s budget and would have stuck the taxpayers of Washington County with the bill. Following outreach from the Oregon delegation, NRSC honored its commitment and released the final sum to TSWCD.
“When Oregonians make a promise, we keep it. The federal government should be held to the same standard,” said Rep. Salinas. “Tualatin Soil and Water did the work to improve our waterways, and Washington County taxpayers should never have been left holding the bag. I’m glad we got this money out the door and where it belongs.”
“Supporting threatened species and their habitats reflects Oregon values and our commitment to environmental protection, and I was grateful when the Tualatin Soil and Water Conservation District secured federal funds to improve fish habitat in Washington County,” said Rep. Bonamici. “Unfortunately, the Trump administration paid only about half of the promised funding, leaving Washington County taxpayers to pick up the balance. I’m glad that my colleagues and I were able to help resolve this issue and secure all the funds the water conservation district needed for the project."
“Thanks to our efforts, this funding is finally moving forward and will help ensure the Tualatin Soil and Water Conservation District can continue its work to improve waterways in Washington County,” said Sen. Merkley. “Oregon’s native fish are the lifeblood of our state, supporting the health and vitality of our communities, local economies, and Tribes who have been here since time immemorial. I’ll keep pushing to secure the necessary federal funds to protect our state’s ecosystems for generations to come.”
“I’m glad the full-court press by the delegation unlocked these resources promised by the federal government to the Tualatin Soil and Water Conservation District,” Wyden said. “These funds will keep waterways improvements on track, helping with water quality and fish habitat alike in Washington County.”
“The Tualatin Soil and Water Conservation District much appreciates Congresswoman Salinas and her staff for their work in helping the District receive payment from the U.S. Department of Agriculture for a successful fish habitat project in the Gales Creek watershed of Washington County,” said Dean P. Moberg, Tualatin Soil and Water Conservation District Treasurer. “We were impressed with the staff's quick understanding of the payment problem we faced, and we are grateful for the Congresswoman's exceptional response. The letter Congresswoman Salinas provided, along with Congresswoman Bonamici and Senators Merkley and Wyden, was surely instrumental in cutting through red tape and securing the payment of over one half million dollars in federal assistance that had been held up for this project. This payment will greatly facilitate the Tualatin Soil and Water Conservation District's work in helping residents of Washington County conserve natural resources with voluntary and locally led projects.
title: Salinas, Bonamici, Merkley, Wyden Secure over $500,000 for Tualatin Soil and Water Conservation District

- For Immediate Release:
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today issued final guidance for manufacturers of cellular and gene therapy (CGT) products to implement a comprehensive, science- and risk-based plan for making sure their products meet potency standards. The guidance provides FDA’s recommendations for a Potency Assurance Strategy, which guides manufacturers to test and verify — before a product reaches a patient — that every batch meets a defined standard of potency to do what the product is supposed to do therapeutically.
The Potency Assurance for Cellular and Gene Therapy Products final guidance replaces FDA's 2011 potency testing guidance for CGT products and applies to treatments for serious and often life-threatening conditions. By law, manufacturers are expected to verify that their products work as intended, from the time of approval through post-approval monitoring. This final guidance provides FDA’s current thinking and recommendations on how manufacturers can meet that requirement.
"Patients who receive cellular and gene therapies are often battling serious or life-threatening conditions, such as cancers and rare diseases, and they deserve the assurance that the product administered to them will perform as intended," said Karim Mikhail, B. Pharm., M.S., Director of the Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research. "This guidance reflects the FDA's commitment to ensuring America remains the best place in the world to innovate — and that innovation is matched by the highest standards of product quality and patient safety."
The guidance provides flexible, risk-based recommendations for manufacturers on how to integrate potency considerations at every stage of development and commercialization — from early-phase investigational new drug (IND) submissions through biologics license application (BLA) approval and continued post-market verification. Key topics include controls for variability in raw materials, testing during manufacturing, and lab tests that confirm each batch is biologically active in a way that matches its intended therapeutic effect. The guidance also addresses specialized considerations for products with short shelf lives, viral vector gene therapies, and patient-specific therapies.
By giving manufacturers a clear, predictable roadmap, this guidance supports faster access to safe and effective therapies for patients who often have no other treatment options — many of whom receive products made individually for a single person. In doing so, it advances the FDA's public health pillars: protecting patients through rigorous quality standards, promoting innovation by providing regulatory clarity, and reinforcing the integrity of the supply chain for some of the most complex medical products in existence.
The FDA will host a webinar on December 10, 2026, to help stakeholders understand and implement the guidance.
The FDA, an agency within the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, protects the public health by assuring the safety, effectiveness, and security of human and veterinary drugs, vaccines and other biological products for human use, and medical devices. The agency also is responsible for the safety and security of our nation’s food supply, cosmetics, dietary supplements, radiation-emitting electronic products, and for regulating tobacco products.
###
title: November 2, 2026 - FDA Provides Clarity to Support Cell and Gene Therapy Development and Quality

WASHINGTON — Today, the U.S. Small Business Administration (SBA) announced that it closed Fiscal Year (FY) 2026 with $100 billion in capital and related assistance delivered through its flagship programs. Despite a 43-day federal shutdown that halted SBA lending for nearly two months of the fiscal year, the agency guaranteed 62,205 7(a) and 504 loans totaling $39.5 billion - the third-highest lending volume in agency history, building on the agency’s record-setting year in FY 2025. The SBA’s Small Business Investment Company (SBIC) program closed the year with a record $60 billion in combined private capital and SBA leverage. In addition, the SBA disbursed $192 million in disaster loans to help communities recover and obligated $419 million to support counseling, training, and contracting services for America’s entrepreneurs.
“President Trump’s America First agenda is driving historic growth within the small business economy, including record new business formations in 2026. In turn, small businesses are seeking more capital to hire workers, expand facilities, and supercharge growth,” said SBA Administrator Kelly Loeffler. “Despite a federal shutdown that halted SBA lending for nearly two months, the agency delivered its third-highest loan volume on record and closed the year with a record SBIC investment portfolio. And we did that while delivering wins for taxpayers by fighting fraud and restoring prudent lending standards, reversing the Biden Administration’s disregard for statutory requirements of the programs we steward, and their decision to ignore criminal activity in SBA programs. In contrast, the Trump Administration’s Working Family Tax Cuts, deregulation, and fair trade policies reward hard work and investment, instead of punishing those who build Main Street businesses. Through $100 billion in lending, investment capital, disaster relief, and entrepreneurial support, the SBA is delivering for America’s job creators, manufacturers, rural communities, and disaster survivors - helping them grow, rebuild, and strengthen communities nationwide.”
The SBA repeatedly warned that a federal shutdown would sharply constrain access to capital and federal contracting for America’s small businesses. Because the 2025 shutdown froze the 7(a) and 504 programs, SBA could not guarantee an estimated $170 million in loans each business day, totaling roughly $5 billion in financing that otherwise could have been approved during FY26.
Even with that disruption, strong underlying growth in the small business economy continued to drive historic demand for SBA programs and capital. Driven by the Working Families Tax Cuts, fair trade, and deregulation, small businesses across America have started and expanded at record rates throughout 2026. New business formations have exceeded 500,000 in nearly every month this year, while indicators such as the PMI Manufacturing Index show ten straight months of sustained expansion in key sectors.
That growth has translated into historic demand for SBA-backed capital. In FY26, the 7(a) program approved 56,130 loans totaling $32.4 billion, while the 504 program approved 6,075 loans totaling $7.1 billion – a combined 1,350 small business loans each week. The SBA supported over 9,700 startups through the 7(a) and 504 programs, totaling $6.5 billion in financing.
This financing reached the sectors and communities central to the Administration’s economic strength. Lending was strongest in accommodation, retail trade, health care, construction, and manufacturing. Construction and manufacturing businesses received a combined $7 billion through 11,790 7(a) and 504 loans. The SBA also guaranteed 10,314 7(a) and 504 loans totaling $6.5 billion to rural small businesses, expanding access to capital in communities that are essential to America’s domestic production.
Building on that demand, the SBA introduced specialized lending tools to direct capital toward domestic manufacturing, supply-chain resilience, food security, and energy investment. In FY26, the agency approved 149 loans totaling nearly $300 million through its 90% Made in America Guarantee. The new 90% Grocery Guarantee program approved 79 loans totaling $145 million, while the new Manufacturers’ Access to Revolving Credit (MARC) program approved 59 loans totaling $54 million.
As demand for SBA-backed financing grew, so did demand for long-term private investment through the SBIC program. The program closed FY26 with a record $60 billion portfolio in combined private capital and SBA leverage, reflecting continued investor confidence in American entrepreneurs and high-growth small businesses. As part of this record year, the SBA approved 46 new SBIC licenses, cultivating a cohort that is expected to support more than $12 billion in total investment. The agency also approved 35 “Green Light” letters representing conditional pre-approval for SBIC licenses expected to generate another $8 billion in aggregate investment.
The SBA’s FY26 support also extended to communities rebuilding after disaster. The agency approved 5,879 disaster loans totaling $272 million and disbursed 5,371 loans totaling $192 million. Its largest disaster responses supported survivors of Super Typhoon Sinlaku in the Northern Mariana Islands, as well as communities affected by severe winter storms in Mississippi and Tennessee.
To complement capital access and disaster recovery, the SBA obligated $419 million in Entrepreneurial Development Program payments to support its nationwide resource partner network. These investments provide counseling, training, and technical assistance that help entrepreneurs access capital, navigate federal programs, start and grow businesses, and build durable local economies.
# # #
About the U.S. Small Business Administration
The U.S. Small Business Administration helps power the American dream of entrepreneurship. As the leading voice for small businesses within the federal government, the SBA empowers job creators with the resources and support they need to start, grow, and expand their businesses or recover from a declared disaster. It delivers services through an extensive network of SBA field offices and partnerships with public and private organizations. To learn more, visit www.sba.gov.
title: SBA Fuels Main Street Growth with $100 Billion Delivered in FY26

A man who conspired to distribute methamphetamine while possessing a firearm in furtherance of that conspiracy was sentenced to 15 years in federal prison.

Thomas Wolterman, age 50, from Hutchinson, Minnesota, but formerly of Lake City, Iowa, received the prison term after a June 17, 2026, guilty plea to one count of conspiracy to distribute methamphetamine and one count of possessing a firearm in furtherance of a drug trafficking crime.

At the plea hearing, Wolterman admitted that between January 2025 through March 2025, he conspired with others to distribute over a pound of methamphetamine in the Lake City, Iowa, area. As part of that conspiracy, Wolterman possessed and then distributed methamphetamine in Lake City on multiple occasions to an individual cooperating with law enforcement. Following a March 13, 2025, controlled purchase of methamphetamine, law enforcement executed a search warrant on Wolterman’s residence in Lake City. Inside, law enforcement located approximately 120 grams of pure methamphetamine in several baggies, a digital scale, packaging materials, and a loaded Mossberg 183T .410 shotgun. Wolterman admitted receiving the firearm as a “drug trade.”

Wolterman was sentenced in Sioux City by United States District Court Judge Leonard T. Strand. Wolterman was sentenced to 120 months’ imprisonment for one count and 60 months’ imprisonment for the second count, to be run consecutively for a total of 180 months’ imprisonment. He must also serve a five-year term of supervised release after the prison term for each count to be run concurrently. There is no parole in the federal system.

Wolterman is being held in the United States Marshal’s custody until he can be transported to a federal prison.

The case was prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney Patrick T. Greenwood and investigated by the Iowa Division of Narcotics Enforcement, the Carroll County Sheriff’s Office, the Calhoun County Sheriff’s Office, the Fort Dodge Police Department, the Lake City Police Department, the Webster County Sheriff’s Office, the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives, and the Iowa DCI Laboratory.

Court file information at https://ecf.iand.uscourts.gov/cgi-bin/login.pl .

The case file number is 25-cr-3028.

Follow us on X @USAO_NDIA.
title: Man Sentenced to Federal Prison for Conspiracy to Distribute Methamphetamine While Possessing a Loaded Firearm

MUSKOGEE, OKLAHOMA – Christopher J. Wilson, U.S. Attorney for the Eastern District of Oklahoma, announced today that Assistant U.S. Attorney (AUSA) and District Election Officer (DEO) T. Cameron McEwen will lead the Eastern District’s efforts in connection with the Justice Department’s comprehensive strategy today to oversee federal voting protections and investigate potential election fraud for the upcoming November 3, 2026, statewide General Election.

In consultation with Justice Department Headquarters in Washington, AUSA McEwen will oversee all district responses to election day complaints of voting rights concerns, threats of violence to election officials or staff, and election fraud for the Eastern District, comprising twenty-six counties in Eastern, Southeastern, and Southcentral Oklahoma including Adair, Atoka, Bryan, Carter, Cherokee, Choctaw, Coal, Haskell, Hughes, Johnston, Latimer, Le Flore, Love, Marshall, McCurtain, McIntosh, Murray, Muskogee, Okfuskee, Okmulgee, Pittsburg, Pontotoc, Pushmataha, Seminole, Sequoyah, and Wagoner Counties.

The Department of Justice has an important role in deterring and combating discrimination and intimidation at the polls, threats of violence directed at election officials and poll workers, and election fraud. The Department will address these violations wherever they occur. The Department’s longstanding Election Day Program furthers these goals and seeks to ensure public confidence in the electoral process by providing local points of contact within the Department for the public to report possible federal election law violations.

Federal law protects against such crimes as threatening violence against election officials or staff, intimidating or bribing voters, buying and selling votes, impersonating voters, altering vote tallies, stuffing ballot boxes, and marking ballots for voters against their wishes or without their input. It also contains special protections for the rights of voters, and provides that they can vote free from interference, including intimidation, and other acts designed to prevent or discourage people from voting or voting for the candidate of their choice. The Voting Rights Act protects the right of voters to mark their own ballot or to be assisted by a person of their choice.

“The right and ability to vote is the cornerstone of our American democracy,” said United States Attorney Christopher J. Wilson. “We all must ensure that those entitled to participate in the election process can exercise that right if they choose, and those who seek to corrupt it are held accountable. In order to respond to complaints of voting rights concerns and election fraud during the upcoming election, and to ensure such complaints are directed to the appropriate authorities, AUSA McEwen will be on duty in this District while the polls are open. He can be reached by calling 918-684-5174.”

In addition, the FBI will have special agents available in each field office and resident agency throughout the country to receive allegations of election fraud and other election abuses on election day. The FBI National Threat Operations Center can be reached by the public at 1-800-CALL-FBI (1-800-225-5324).

Complaints about possible violations of the federal voting rights laws can be made directly to the Civil Rights Division in Washington, DC, by phone at 1-800-253-3931 or by complaint form at https://civilrights.justice.gov/.

Please note: if you experience violence or intimidation at the polls, please call 911 immediately before contacting federal authorities.
title: United States Attorney Designates Election Officer For The Eastern District Of Oklahoma

HUNTINGTON, W.Va. – Leroy Terrell Newson, also known as “Money,” 36, of Detroit, Michigan, pleaded guilty today to distribution of methamphetamine.

As part of his guilty plea, Newson admitted that he conducted the transaction in his vehicle after arranging it beforehand with the confidential informant by phone. Newson further admitted that he sold approximately 18 grams of methamphetamine on March 16, 2026, approximately 24 grams of methamphetamine on March 26, 2026, and approximately 24 grams of methamphetamine on April 20, 2026. Newson is scheduled to be sentenced on February 22, 2027, and faces a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison, at least three years of supervised release, and a fine of up to $1 million.

Newson was arrested on August 13, 2026, as part of “Operation Coal Country,” a multi-week enforcement initiative that targeted noncompliant sex offenders, individuals wanted for sex crimes, violent fugitives, and other wanted individuals throughout the Southern District of West Virginia.

FAIRVIEW HEIGHTS, Ill. – U.S. Attorney Steven D. Weinhoeft released a statement following a quadruple shooting on Sunday night in Madison and is asking for the public’s help:

On Sunday night, during a youth football championship game at Madison Senior High School, four people were shot. One person was killed at the scene, and three others were taken to area hospitals and are reported in stable condition. The Major Case Squad of Greater St. Louis is leading the investigation, along with the Madison Police Department.

The U.S. Department of Justice has directed all United States Attorneys to ensure a rapid federal response to combat violent crimes, and resources from the U.S. Attorney’s Office, the FBI, the ATF, and the U.S. Marshal’s Service have been directed to assist.

An FBI tip line was created to receive photos and videos from the incident. We are asking the public to share every video and every photo from the incident, even if it did not capture the actual shooting incident. Any photo showing the crowd, clothing and faces could be critical to this investigation. Many of the events are captured on area surveillance cameras, but we need the public’s help to identify those involved. Please upload photos and videos to: https://tips.fbi.gov/digitalmedia/7a3b922a9c889f5 .

Investigators are asking anyone who was at the game to come forward with information. Tips can also be given to the Major Case Squad command post at 618-709-7750 or to Crime Stoppers at 1-866-371-TIPS (8477).

“While watching 12- and 13-year-olds play football, violence erupted and gunshots rang out killing one, injuring three, and creating terror for hundreds,” said United States Attorney Steven D. Weinhoeft. “We don’t have to live like this. Law enforcement working with the community can bring this lawlessness to end. Please help us do so.”

Moms.gov: In May 2026, HHS launched Moms.gov, a website designed to support new and expecting mothers. This new resource offers guidance and information for mothers and fathers who are navigating difficult or unexpected pregnancies to ensure the wellbeing of mothers and healthy American families.
Moms.gov is an easy-to-navigate platform featuring information about pregnancy centers, Federally Qualified Health Centers (FQHCs), nutritional guidance, Trump Accounts, and other resources that support maternal and infant health. Moms.gov delivers on longstanding requests from stakeholders and Members of Congress. Most importantly, Moms.gov prioritizes MAHA and MAGA initiatives, including family formation, nutritional information, and affordability.
There are sections that include the following:
- Support Services and Health Centers (Pregnancy Centers and FQHCs)
- Nutrition Quick Facts for Mothers based on the DGAs
- Trump Accounts
- Trump Rx
- Resources for Women & Parents
- Preconception Health
- Breastfeeding
- Nutrition
- Mental Health
- Adoption
- Early Head Start
- Additional Resources: Child Welfare, Sleep Safety, Substance Use, Infections, Health Conditions, and Additional Exposures.
