PICATINNY ARSENAL, N.J. - With decades of fuze experience and knowhow at risk of disappearing as engineers begin to transition out, the U.S. Army Combat Capabilities Development Command (DEVCOM) Armaments Center has stepped up to the task of readying the workforce.
Between Monday, Oct. 19 and Friday, Oct. 23, the Armaments Center hosted a course related to munition fuzes for 30 business professionals from small and big business alike. Taught by Senior Fuze Subject Matter Expert Tom Emanski, Acting Army Fuze Management Office Chief Sandy Picinic, Army Fuze Safety Review Board Executive Secretary Briar Ostar-Exel and Armaments Center Fuze Division Engineer Lam Vo, the course provided an open forum for engineers to examine the fundamentals of fuze design, safety philosophies, operational environments and emerging threats, while engaging directly with the experts who help shape military safety standards and evaluations. Fuzes, being the component in a munition that decides when and under what conditions the warhead should function, are a critical component in munitions directly responsible for providing both safety to the warfighter and down range lethality.
According to Emanski, the course was conceived after industrial partners repeatedly signaled how few options there were to learn about fuzing in academia. The field is very rarely taught in traditional academic programs, so many professionals must learn the fundamentals on the job, and while the Armaments Center’s Armament Graduate School (AGS) does have a fuze elective, it is only open to students at the school, making it difficult to preserve knowledge as prior subject matter experts in industry begin to retire. Built from the elective, the course provided training to help both new hires and established professionals develop a shared foundation on fuzes and pass their knowledge forward.
The National Armaments Consortium helped advertise, process applications and coordinate logistics, and Emanski, Picinic and Vo signed on as instructors as they already supported a related elective at AGS. Though the course was planned for some time, it only took about nine weeks to screen applicants and select attendees, Emanski said. The course was capped to 30 students to preserve interactive two-way discussion and deep learning, as any larger would approach a lecture.
“It’s to help as a starting point to understand this very unique item called ‘fuze’, which plays a critical role in our munitions,” noted Picinic.
During the course, attendees received a basic overview of fuzes, delved into the fundamentals of fuze safety design architectures and environments, discussed hand-placed ordnance, target detection, among other topics. The syllabus also addressed the ever-changing landscape of unmanned systems, in which fuzes are a quintessential component, and explained both electronic and mechanical aspects.
“Fuzes are on just about every munition out there. It’s challenging to teach a course when there’s so many use cases,” said Emanski. “Each fuze for every commodity item is different, so we’re teaching a course where there are many different examples, use cases and CONOPs (concepts of operation).”
The students themselves came from both small and large businesses; some had a decade of experience with fuzes, while others had never touched one before. This spectrum of experience, alongside the wide variety in business backgrounds, led to meaningful engagement throughout the week.
“My group designs and builds seekers and tracking missile interceptors. We're expanding our capabilities, and this was an area identified as a key gap where we wanted to deepen our expertise,” said Boeing Integrated Air and Missile Defense engineer Erik Stein.
Several students noted not only the broad omnibus, but how different the course was from what they expected. Falcata AI Engineer Adam Tuck showed surprise at spending a full day talking about interrupted fuzes, which use purely mechanical components to keep the fuze from setting a munition off too early, and non-interrupted fuzes, which use electronics. Wild West Systems Chief Engineer of Munitions and Energetics John Granier called the discussion about balancing cost and safety “fascinating,” while TETAC Incorporated Chief Executive Officer Mark Benson noted the section on fuze safety boards and how it humanized a force usually unseen.
Participants praised the course universally for offering information otherwise not available to industry and expressed hope that a similar course would be offered again in the future.
“I think a lot of the reason why this is so niche is that there’s no awareness of this at the collegiate level. It’d be cool, now that we’re opening this up to industry, if that eventually bleeds down to universities and maybe gets more people interested earlier on rather than as we go through our careers. I didn’t know what a fuze was when I started,” said Day and Zimmermann Munitions Director of Business Development Christopher Stemple.
According to Emanski, there have already been inquiries from industry members about when the Armaments Center can offer the course again in the future. Seeing the success of the course, the Armaments Center has already started working with NAC representatives and industry to expand the course offering in 2027.
title: Armaments Center hosts first industry fuzing course to preserve critical expertise

Comisionado Residente presenta comentarios sobre las reglas propuestas para el Censo 2030 y su impacto en Puerto Rico
Los comentarios profundizan en las preocupaciones expresadas por el Comisionado Residente al firmar, junto a otros miembros del Congreso, una carta el 30 de octubre que solicitó retirar la propuesta.
Caguas, Puerto Rico — El Comisionado Residente Pablo José Hernández presentó comentarios ante el Negociado del Censo de Estados Unidos para advertir sobre los posibles efectos de las reglas propuestas para el Censo 2030 en la contabilización de la población de Puerto Rico y de las comunidades puertorriqueñas en Estados Unidos.
El 30 de octubre, Hernández firmó junto a otros miembros del Congreso una carta dirigida al Negociado del Censo en la que expresaron su oposición a la propuesta y solicitaron su retiro. La comunicación planteó preocupaciones sobre los nuevos criterios de residencia, el uso de récords administrativos y las restricciones a la recopilación de información sobre raza, origen étnico y orientación sexual. En sus comentarios específicos sobre Puerto Rico, el Comisionado Residente detalla cómo estos cambios podrían afectar el conteo de nuestra población.
“Nos preocupa que esta propuesta limite la información demográfica esencial que se recopila sobre nuestra población. Sin datos precisos, se hace más difícil identificar las necesidades de nuestras comunidades y priorizar lo básico: los servicios, los recursos y la atención que nuestra gente necesita. Por eso, me opuse a esta regla y solicité su retiro”, expresó el Comisionado Residente.
Entre sus señalamientos, Hernández advierte que utilizar únicamente récords contributivos federales podría excluir a residentes bona fide de Puerto Rico que no tienen obligación de radicar una planilla federal. Por ello, plantea considerar también información del Departamento de Hacienda, incluidos los formularios W-2PR. Asimismo, señala que los sistemas automatizados podrían dejar fuera hogares en comunidades rurales cuyas direcciones no siguen los formatos convencionales.
Los comentarios también cuestionan las posibles restricciones a las preguntas sobre raza y origen hispano, cuya información permite identificar a las comunidades puertorriqueñas dentro y fuera de la Isla. Además, señalan la importancia de considerar los movimientos de personas entre Puerto Rico y los estados para evitar que sean omitidas o contadas incorrectamente.
La importancia de un conteo preciso queda reflejada en los resultados de 2020. Según el propio Negociado del Censo, en el Censo de 2020 se estima que aproximadamente 217,000 residentes de Puerto Rico, equivalentes al 7.1% de la población estimada en hogares, fueron omitidos del conteo.
Los datos del Censo ayudan al Gobierno de Puerto Rico a planificar los servicios que necesitan los municipios y las comunidades, revisar los distritos legislativos y administrar programas federales. Por eso, Hernández plantea que las reglas del Censo 2030 deben evitar que Puerto Rico y su población queden insuficientemente representados en la información oficial.
###
title: Comisionado Residente presenta comentarios sobre las reglas propuestas para el Censo 2030 y su impacto en Puerto Rico

Tallahassee, Florida — The Department of Justice’s Office on Violence Against Women has awarded a $400,000 federal grant to Florida State University to support on-campus approaches to combat domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault, and stalking. United States Attorney John P. Heekin highlighted the recently announced award following the conclusion of Domestic Violence Awareness Month that took place during October 2026.

U.S. Attorney John P. Heekin said: “October was Domestic Violence Awareness Month, but our efforts to provide safety, dignity, and justice to victims and survivors of domestic violence continue year-round. Through this critical investment of federal grant monies, we provide vital resources to FSU’s on-campus programs that ensure victim safety and assistance while holding offenders accountable. Together, we can put an end to domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault, and stalking on campus.”

The award, paid through the Office on Violence Against Women Fiscal Year 2025 Grants to Reduce Domestic Violence, Dating Violence, Sexual Assault, and Stalking On Campus Program, provides institutions of higher education the resources to establish multidisciplinary approaches to combat domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault, and stalking on campuses. The Campus Program supports comprehensive approaches designed to enhance victim services (including legal services), implement prevention and education programs, and develop and strengthen security and investigation strategies to prevent, prosecute, and respond to domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault, and stalking.

The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Florida is committed to prosecuting those who violate federal laws, collaborating with local & campus law enforcement, and ensuring victims have access to the resources they need. By understanding the signs of abuse and connecting victims to resources, we can all play a role in creating safer communities. For more information on domestic violence or to access resources, please visit https://www.justice.gov/ovw/domestic-violence .

The Department of Justice funds essential victim services through its grantmaking. Grantees of OVW and the Department’s Office for Victims of Crime (OVC) run programs that support victims in the aftermath of domestic violence. There is help available, including the National Domestic Violence Hotline, 1-800-799-SAFE (7233), and the Strong Hearts Native Helpline, 1-844-7NATIVE (762-8483). In addition, OVW’s Resources for Victims and Survivors webpage lists national hotlines as well as state, territorial, and Tribal domestic violence and sexual assault coalitions that can direct victims to local resources and services, as well as opportunities to get involved.

To access public court documents online, please visit the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Florida website. For more information about the United States Attorney’s Office, Northern District of Florida, visit https://www.justice.gov/usao-ndfl .

text: St. Thomas, USVI –United States Attorney Adam Sleeper announced today that Assistant United States Attorney Erik Tate has been appointed to serve as the District Election Officer and, in that capacity, will be responsible for overseeing the District’s handling of election day complaints related to voting rights concerns, threats of violence to election officials or staff, and election fraud. The Department of Justice has an important role in deterring and combatting discrimination and intimidation at the polls, threats of violence directed at election officials and poll workers, and election fraud and will address these violations wherever they occur. The Department’s longstanding Election Day Program furthers these goals and seeks to ensure public confidence in the electoral process by providing local points of contact within the Department for the public to report possible federal election law violations. “Every citizen must be free to cast his or her vote without interference or discrimination,” United States Attorney Sleeper said. “The Department of Justice will work tirelessly to protect the integrity of the election process.” Federal law protects against such crimes as threatening violence against election officials or staff, intimidating or bribing voters, buying and selling votes, impersonating voters, altering vote tallies, voting by non-citizens, stuffing ballot boxes, and marking ballots for voters against their wishes or without their input. It also contains special protections for the rights of voters, and provides that they can vote free from interference, including intimidation, and other acts designed to prevent or discourage people from voting or voting for the candidate of their choice. The Voting Rights Act protects the right of voters to mark their own ballot or to be assisted by a person of their choice (where voters need assistance because of disability or inability to read or write in English). Assistant United States Attorney Tate and other Assistant United States Attorneys will be on duty in this District while the polls are open and can be reached by the public at 340-774-5757. The FBI will also have special agents available to receive allegations of election fraud and other election abuses on election day. The FBI can be reached by the public at 787-987-6500. Complaints about possible violations of the federal voting rights laws can also be made directly to the Civil Rights Division in Washington, DC by phone at (855) 856-1247 (toll free) or by complaint form at https://civilrights.justice.gov/electionintegrity .
title: United States Attorney Names District Election Officer to Oversee Election Day Complaints

WASHINGTON – The U.S. Department of the Treasury today announced its current estimates of privately-held net marketable borrowing for the October–December 2026 and January–March 2027 quarters.
- During the October–December 2026 quarter, Treasury expects to borrow $618 billion in privately-held net marketable debt, assuming an end-of-December cash balance of $850 billion. The borrowing estimate is $10 billion lower than announced in August 2026, primarily due to the higher-than-assumed beginning of quarter cash balance, partially offset by lower projected net cash flows. Excluding the higher-than-assumed beginning-of-quarter cash balance, the current quarter borrowing estimate is $24 billion higher than announced in August.
- During the January–March 2027 quarter, Treasury expects to borrow $800 billion in privately-held net marketable debt, assuming an end-of-March cash balance of $1.000 trillion.
- During the July–September 2026 quarter, Treasury borrowed $742 billion in privately-held net marketable debt and ended the quarter with a cash balance of $984 billion. In August 2026, Treasury estimated borrowing of $739 billion and assumed an end-of-September cash balance of $950 billion. The $4 billion in higher privately-held net marketable borrowing resulted primarily from the higher-than-assumed end-of-quarter cash balance, offset by higher net cash flows. Excluding the higher-than-assumed end-of-quarter cash balance, actual borrowing was $30 billion lower than announced in August.
Additional financing details relating to Treasury’s Quarterly Refunding will be released at 8:30 a.m. on Wednesday, November 4, 2026.
###
1. Privately-held net marketable borrowing excludes rollovers (auction “add-ons”) of Treasury securities held in the SOMA but includes financing required due to SOMA redemptions. Secondary market purchases of Treasury securities by SOMA do not directly change privately-held net marketable borrowing but, all else equal, when the securities mature and assuming the Federal Reserve does not redeem any maturing securities, would increase the amount of cash raised for a given privately-held auction size by increasing the SOMA “add-on” amount. Additionally, buybacks are not expected to significantly affect privately-held net marketable borrowing as new issuance replaces securities that are bought back.

The Department of the Air Force’s Spark Tank program concludes its final year with the Top 5 ideas selected out of 350 total submissions. These ideas endured strict subject matter evaluation from 1,394 members casting nearly 26,000 votes, evaluation from command leadership, and final determination by a panel of innovation leaders.
Out of 350 total submissions from across the Air and Space Forces, the Spark Tank 2026 Top 5 are:
Automated Master Storage Plan (Air Combat Command) – Leverages artificial intelligence to plan warehouse layouts for munitions, enabling weeks of planning to be executed in minutes.
M-UAS-D, MANET-enabled UAS Detector (Air Combat Command) – Low-cost for large scale deployment, a counter sUAS to detect drones, share real-time range data to users and response teams.
Project CAPYBARA (Air Mobility Command) – A set of tutorials and parts lists provided to any organization to build custom rovers for any capability needed in the field, replacing costly TDYs and certification programs.
Secure STIG Checker (Air Force Special Operations Command) – Replaces Enterprise Network manual compliance checks with a tool capable of analyzing millions of lines of code in under 500 seconds.
Tac-Hub: Agile Communications for the Modern Mission (Air Force Global Strike Command) – Modular command and control suite to enable rapid deployment; designed for military and emergency response teams.
Spark Tank is the Department of the Air Force's premier campaign where Guardians and Airmen present their innovative solutions to top leaders and industry experts, seeking sponsorship to bring their concepts to life.
The Top 5 teams will now accelerate prototypes and forge strategic partnerships with the help of AFWERX Refinery and DAF Enterprise Innovation support.
A panel of judges also reviewed the following semi-finalist submissions, which will be migrated for support and progression:
Aerial Minefield (Air Combat Command) – Low cost solution to create dense clouds of aerial obstacles to defend against and disable low-cost adversarial drones.
Agile Cyber Training Environment: Portable Cyber Ops Center (Air Combat Command) – Portable, battery-powered, network-independent center globally deployable by a single person in less than a minute for agile cyber operations.
Contingency Remote Optical Charging Spacecraft (Space Systems Group) – Charges dead spacecraft with ground lasers to prevent abandoned spacecraft and lost satellites due to loss of power.
Energy Resilience Command Platform (Air Force Reserve Command) – Dashboard unifying all base energy, power, water, heating, and mission critical data into a real time “Base Resilience Percentage”, indicating operational sustainment during disruptions.
Flight Room 3D Models (Air Education and Training Command) – Standardizes and institutionalizes 3D printed models of pilot curriculum items.
Project HOPLITE (Air Force Special Operations Command) – Integrates key components from Land Phalanx Weapon System, tactical truck, or FMTV load handling system to create a flexible and rapidly deployable air defense solution, transportable by C-130.
(ReSearch) an Advanced Search Engine for EPubs (Air Force Material Command) – Integrates Advana’s advanced search engine, natural language processing, and data analytics into the EPubs platform to allow Airmen to find exactly what they are looking for.
SpartReg 36-2903 Pictures of Dress Right vs. Wrong (Pacific Air Forces) – Digital interactive guide with side-by-side “correct vs. incorrect” examples, hyperlinks, and visual decision trees for dress and appearance standards.
Streamline 1205 Narrative Sync (Pacific Air Forces) – Standardize Air Force writing style by switching from character count format that matches EPB/ORB narrative standards.
The Sheppard Blueprint: A Proven Model for CONUS MTF Pharmacy Recapture (Air Education and Training Command) – Low-cost and highly replicable, a text message outreach and 24/7 prescription lockers to prevent lost cost in on-base pharmacies.
Vehicle Diagnostic System (Air National Guard) – Consolidates 5 tools and 7 software licenses into 1 tool for vehicle diagnostics.
title: DAF announces Spark Tank 2026 Top 5

Gainesville, Florida – Samonta Leondre James, 26, of Gainesville, Florida, has pleaded guilty in federal court on a charge of possession of a firearm and ammunition by a convicted felon. John P. Heekin, United States Attorney for the Northern District of Florida announced the guilty plea.

U.S. Attorney Heekin said: “I applaud the excellent investigative work by the Gainesville Police Department to remove this dangerous felon from our streets. My office will continue to aggressively prosecute these offenders to make abundantly clear that the Northern District of Florida has zero-tolerance from crime.”

According to court records, Gainesville Police Department conducted a traffic stop on a vehicle where the Defendant was a passenger. When asked by law enforcement if he had any weapons, the defendant stated that he had a firearm in his possession. A search of the defendant uncovered a Glock 29 10-millimeter handgun with seven rounds of ammunition. The defendant has prior convictions for Possession with Intent to Sell Cannabis within 1000 Feet of a Place of Worship and Possession with Intent to Sell Cannabis, and he is legally prohibited from possessing a firearm and ammunition.

Sentencing is scheduled for February 16, 2027, at 1:30pm before Chief United States District Court Judge Allen Winsor in Gainesville, Florida. The Defendant faces up to 15 years’ imprisonment.

The case was jointly investigated by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, and the Gainesville Police Department. The case is being prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney Tyler Fleming.

Project Safe Neighborhoods (PSN) is the Department of Justice’s nationwide initiative that brings federal, state, local, and tribal law enforcement, prosecutors, and other public safety partners together to coordinate efforts to combat violent crime and make communities safe. Coordinated by U.S. Attorneys’ offices in each of the 94 federal districts, PSN is tailored to particular communities to strategically address specific violent crime and public safety challenges. As a key component of Operation Take Back America, PSN serves a central role in the Department’s commitment to make our country safe. PSN emphasizes three core principles: rapid federal response to violent crime and criminal offenders; strong, strategic partnerships among law enforcement at all levels; and accountability and deterrence through the prosecution of the most serious, readily provable offenses and other strategies. These efforts complement and strengthen President Trump’s Homeland Security Task Forces, ensuring a comprehensive federal response to the most pressing public safety issues facing communities .

MUSKOGEE, OKLAHOMA – The United States Attorney’s Office for the Eastern District of Oklahoma announced that Leobaldo Espinoza-Hinojosa, age 45, a Mexican national unlawfully present in LeFlore County, Oklahoma, pleaded guilty to one count of Unlawful Reentry of Removed Alien, punishable by a term of imprisonment of not more than ten years, and a fine of not more than $250,000.00.

The charge arose from an investigation by the U.S. Department of Homeland Security’s Immigration and Customs Enforcement Division and the Arkoma Police Department.

The Indictment alleged that on September 18, 2026, Espinoza-Hinojosa, an alien, was found in Arkoma, Oklahoma, without obtaining the express consent of the Secretary of Homeland Security to reapply for admission to the United States after having been previously removed on July 13, 2006.

This case is part of Operation Take Back America , a nationwide initiative that marshals the full resources of the Department of Justice to repel the invasion of illegal immigration, achieve the total elimination of cartels and transnational criminal organizations (TCOs), and protect our communities from the perpetrators of violent crime.

The Honorable Gerald L. Jackson, Magistrate Judge in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Oklahoma, accepted the plea and ordered the completion of a presentence investigation report.

A U.S. District Court Judge will determine the sentence to be imposed after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors.

Espinoza-Hinojosa will remain in the custody of the United States Marshals Service pending sentencing.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Chuck Sullivan represented the United States.

MONROE – On October 21, 2026, United States Chief District Judge Terry A. Doughty sentenced Justavious K. “Tae Tae” Williams , 25, of Bastrop, to 336 months in federal prison for Conspiracy to Possess a Controlled Substance with Intent to Distribute and for Possessing a Firearm in Furtherance of a Drug Trafficking Crime, followed by five years of supervised release. Williams previously pled guilty to the charges on July 10, 2026.

According to court documents, between May 16, 2025, and October 9, 2025, Williams participated in a methamphetamine trafficking organization. Investigators executed a wiretap on one of Williams’ co-conspirator’s phones and intercepted calls and messages in which Williams discussed acquiring and distributing large quantities of methamphetamine. On October 1, 2025, communications revealed that Williams’ co-conspirators were arranging the pickup of a large shipment of methamphetamine from Texas. Williams then traveled to Garland, Texas, where agents observed him and a co-conspirator load a bright orange suitcase into a vehicle. After the vehicle returned to Louisiana, Louisiana State Police (LSP) later attempted a traffic stop. Williams fled the stop, leading troopers on a brief pursuit before Williams and the co-conspirator were caught and arrested. A search of the vehicle revealed approximately 25 kilograms of methamphetamine in the suitcase. Roughly a week later, Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) agents executed a search warrant at a local address where Williams was found with the same co-conspirator as in the car stop. Inside the residence, agents recovered seven firearms along with various quantities of ecstasy pills, methamphetamine, marijuana, and other controlled substances. A cook lab trailer located behind the residence contained 20,000 methamphetamine pills and more than three kilograms of additional powder methamphetamine.

U.S. Attorney Zachary A. Keller for the Western District of Louisiana made the announcement.

The case was investigated by DEA, LSP, and Monroe Metro Narcotics. It was prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney J. Aaron Crawford with assistance from Legal Assistant Amanda Morgan.

You may find a copy of this press release (and any updates) at www.justice.gov/usao-wdla.

Related court documents and information may be found on the website of the District Court for the Western District of Louisiana at www.lawd.uscourts.gov or at https://www.lawd.uscourts.gov/cmecf-pacer, under Case Number 3:25 cr 299.

FORT WAINWRIGHT, Alaska — From hand-sewn prototypes to custom-built web platforms, Soldiers of the 11th Airborne Division demonstrated the power of grassroots innovation during Angel Ascent, held Oct. 28 at the division theater.
Col. Matthew Adamczyk, Deputy Commanding Officer for Operations, 11th Airborne Division, praised the competitors’ efforts.
“Soldiers across the 11th Airborne Division continue to demonstrate that many of the best ideas come from the bottom up. Events like Angel Ascent prove the ability of our troops to solve problems, our job is to help provide the right resources. When our Soldiers and leaders are empowered, there's no limit to what we can achieve in the Arctic and beyond.” said Col. Adamczyk.
Spc. Leighton Keilen, 1st Battalion, 24th Infantry Regiment, 1st Infantry Brigade Combat Team, 11th Airborne Division, earned first place for his Skydio Drone Relay and modular payload delivery system that significantly extends tactical drone range and utility in Alaska’s rugged, mountainous terrain. Col. Matthew Adamczyk presented Keilen with a Meritorious Service Medal. All other competitors received Army Commendation Medals, and every participant was awarded a four-day pass in recognition of their efforts.
The competition provided Soldiers of all ranks a direct platform to present practical solutions to senior military leaders, civilian officials and innovation experts. Each innovator received 10 minutes to brief their project followed by five minutes of questions from the judging panel, which evaluated entries on problem identification, solution quality, operational value, resource requirements and presentation.
The event highlighted a key truth: some of the Army’s most effective solutions come from the Soldiers who live with the problems every day. Whether serving in Arctic extremes or supporting complex administrative demands, these warfighters refused to accept “the way it’s always been done.”
The competitors’ backgrounds highlight the wide range of skills, experiences and perspectives that strengthen today’s Army. Pfc. Michael Pereira, a Tactical Unmanned Aircraft Systems specialist from Miami, Florida, hand-sewed his first prototype of a passive thermal battery vault designed to keep drone batteries viable in sub-zero temperatures using only body heat and radiant barriers. Staff Sgt. Baddeley, a respiratory therapist from Petaluma, California, developed TroopToTask.org after years of watching small-unit leaders struggle with fragmented spreadsheets. His intuitive web platform consolidates personnel data, training records, duty rosters and mission tracking, allowing commanders, first sergeants and leaders at every echelon to focus on leading Soldiers instead of chasing administrative tasks.
Other standout projects included a low-cost battery eliminator for PRC-158 radios in extreme cold, a modular power and heating system for man-hauled Ahkio sleds, 3D-printed explosively formed penetrators for FPV drones, and a unit-fabricated ring mount hatch for FMTVs that protects convoy gunners in Arctic conditions for a fraction of the cost of commercial systems.
By formally recognizing these efforts with awards and command emphasis, the 11th Airborne Division is cultivating a culture where initiative is expected and innovation is accelerated. Events like Angel Ascent serve as a powerful example for the broader Army of how to empower Soldiers at the tactical edge to solve real problems, reduce logistical burdens, and increase lethality in austere environments.
title: Soldiers from across 11th Airborne Division shine at Angel Ascent innovation competition

Payment processor Riverside Payments Inc., its affiliate Cascade Equipment Leasing LLC and their operators will pay $600,000 to resolve Federal Trade Commission and Washington state allegations that the firms deceived small businesses by falsely promising to save them money on payment processing services and making it nearly impossible to cancel despite offering “risk-free” cancellation.
Small businesses also will be able to rescind processing agreements without a termination penalty under the proposed order settling the FTC and Washington’s allegations.
In their complaint, the FTC and the State of Washington allege that Washington-based Riverside, Cascade and their owners and executives, Brandon Skinner and Jason Reese, falsely promised small businesses that they would save money on payment-processing services, while failing to clearly inform the businesses that they were being enrolled in automatically renewing contracts for payment-processing services and to lease equipment.
“Riverside and Cascade promised small businesses significant savings, but instead of saving money locked them into costly, multi-year contracts and made it very difficult to cancel,” said Christopher Mufarrige, Director of the FTC’s Bureau of Consumer Protection. “The FTC will hold accountable companies that deceive small businesses, whose hard work powers our economy.”
The FTC and Washington allege that Riverside’s sales pitches included a quote sheet that compared the costs prospective clients paid their existing payment processor with the amount they would save if they used Riverside’s services instead. The complaint alleges that Riverside at times claimed that small businesses could save 40% to 60% by switching to Riverside. In reality, the FTC and Washington allege, small businesses who switched to Riverside typically ended up paying more than they did with their previous provider.
The quote sheet Riverside provided to potential clients failed to include various fees, such as activation fees, batch fees and fees for supposed non-compliance with data security standards or inactive processing, according to the complaint. In addition, Riverside’s 26-page electronic contract buried key information not clearly disclosed by sales agents, according to the complaint. This included information about automatic renewals for processing services after the initial three-year term; a $695 early termination fee; and the cost of leasing payment processing machines from Cascade, which locked customers into an auto-renewing contract that lasted one year longer than the processing contract.
The FTC and Washington allege that Riverside made it extremely difficult for small businesses to cancel it services despite its promised “no-risk” guarantee when customers signed up. The company not only falsely promised businesses they could cancel anytime without penalty but also falsely claimed that it would switch unsatisfied businesses back to their original payment processor and pay them $500 for their “time and hassle.”
The complaint alleges that small businesses who attempted to cancel typically did not hear back from Riverside and were often stuck in a loop of fruitless phone calls and deflection.
Even businesses that were willing to pay Riverside’s improperly disclosed $695 termination fee, which was a surprise to many, were told there was no direct line to call to cancel Riverside’s services and they must wait to receive a call back. The complaint alleges that such callbacks often never came.
In addition, the FTC and Washington allege that Riverside has made false and unsubstantiated claims about how much money its sales agents, who work on commission, will earn. Riverside’s ads have claimed sales agents could earn between $75,000 and $95,000 a year, and that top sales agents can make “100k.” In reality, agents made, on average, just $3,787 per year, according to the complaint.
The FTC alleges that Riverside’s practices violated the FTC Act and the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act by obtaining consumers’ financial information by using false or fraudulent statements.
The proposed order resolving the FTC’s and Washington’s allegations imposes a $32,083,921 judgment against Riverside, Skinner, Reese and Cascade, which will be suspended after payment of $600,000 due to their inability to pay the full amount. The full amount will be due if they are found to have lied about their finances.
The order also requires the defendants to notify their customers that Riverside will, for a 60-day period, waive the early termination fee or any penalty for rescinding the merchant-processing agreements. The defendants also will be prohibited from: misrepresenting the costs, savings, cancellation conditions or any other material fact about any good or service they sell; making unsubstantiated claims about the amount of savings customers will realize; making unsubstantiated earnings claims; and misrepresenting any aspect of a negative option feature related to a good or service they sell.
The order also requires the defendants to clearly and conspicuously disclose to consumers, prior to obtaining their billing information, all material terms of the transaction, to obtain consumers’ express informed consent to use a negative option plan to bill consumers and to provide consumers with a simple way to cancel a negative option plan.
The Commission vote authorizing the staff to file the complaint and stipulated final order was 2-0. The FTC and Washington filed the complaint and final order in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Washington.
NOTE: The Commission files a complaint when it has “reason to believe” that the named defendants are violating or are about to violate the law and it appears to the Commission that a proceeding is in the public interest. Stipulated final orders have the force of law when approved and signed by the District Court judge.
The Federal Trade Commission works to promote competition and protect and educate consumers. The FTC will never demand money, make threats, tell you to transfer money, or promise you a prize. Learn more about consumer topics at consumer.ftc.gov, or report fraud, scams, and bad business practices at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. Follow the FTC on social media, read consumer alerts and the business blog, and sign up to get the latest FTC news and alerts.
title: FTC, Washington Take Action Against Payment Processor for Deceiving Small Businesses About Costs and Cancellation Terms

STATESBORO, Georgia: A Candler County man has been sentenced to federal prison for methamphetamine distribution.

The sentence was imposed by U.S. District Court Judge J. Randal Hall and announced by Margaret E. “Meg” Heap, U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Georgia.

Nakia Donaldson , 36, of Metter, was sentenced to 192 months in prison and a $2,000 fine followed by four years of supervised release after pleading guilty to Distribution of Methamphetamine.

There is no parole in the federal system.

According to court documents and testimony, in 2024, the Georgia Bureau of Investigation (GBI) initiated an investigation into the distribution of methamphetamine by Donaldson.

During a July 2024 controlled purchase, investigators used covert electronic recording devices to capture Donaldson selling nine ounces of methamphetamine to undercover agents for $1,400. Testing conducted later by the GBI Division of Forensic Science at the Coastal Regional Lab confirmed the presence of methamphetamine.

Donaldson’s co-defendants, Efram Todd Donaldson , 57, of Metter, was sentenced to 48 months in prison and a $2,000 fine followed by three years of supervised release, and Justin E. Aldrich , 40, of Metter, was sentenced to time served and a $1,500 fine followed by three years of supervised release after both defendants pled guilty to Distribution of Methamphetamine.

"Our communities are significantly safer today because federal and local law enforcement moved quickly to sever this supply chain," said U.S. Attorney Heap. "By intercepting this defendant with a significant amount of methamphetamine, the GBI effectively cut off a toxic pipeline pouring into Metter. Let this serve as a clear warning that we will aggressively pursue and dismantle trafficking operations at every level."

The case was investigated by the Georgia Bureau of Investigation and local law enforcement agencies.

“This sentencing is the result of excellent undercover work that exposed a dangerous drug distribution operation,” said GBI Director Chris Hosey. “The GBI worked alongside our law enforcement partners to stop the flow of methamphetamine into the local community, and we will continue to pursue those who bring dangerous drugs into the communities we serve.”

This case was prosecuted for the United States by Southern District of Georgia Assistant U.S. Attorneys L. Alexander Hamner and Darron J. Hubbard.
title: Defendant sentenced to 16 years in prison after pleading guilty to drug distribution charges

TULSA, Okla. – A native and citizen of the Philippines, Maria Elenor Lopez Rios, 45, and a lawful permanent resident of the United States, was charged by Criminal Complaint in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Oklahoma with falsely claiming U.S. citizenship, making false statements in relation to voter registration, submitting a fraudulent voter registration, and unlawfully voting in a federal election. Rios was arrested today pursuant to the complaint.

“Free and fair elections depend on the integrity of our voter registration and election systems,” said U.S. Attorney Christopher Nassar. “When individuals falsely claim U.S. citizenship to register or vote, they undermine the public’s trust in those systems and dilute the votes of American citizens. Our office will continue to work with our law‑enforcement partners to safeguard the election process and ensure that only those legally eligible to vote are able to do so.”

According to the complaint, Department of Homeland Security records show that Rios entered the United States in 2017 and has never been a United States citizen. In March 2022, Rios allegedly registered to vote in Tulsa County, falsely affirming under penalty of perjury that she was a U.S. citizen. On Rios’s application for naturalization paperwork in March 2026, she allegedly claimed she had never voted, nor claimed to be a U.S. citizen. Voter registration records reflect that she voted in the November 2022, federal midterm election in Broken Arrow, Oklahoma.

The charges arise from an investigation initiated after the Tulsa County Election Board referred several instances where non‑citizens were removed from jury duty lists because of indications they were not U.S. citizens. Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) Tulsa reviewed these referrals and determined that Rios had both registered to vote and cast a ballot despite her immigration status prohibiting her from lawfully doing so.

If convicted, Rios faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison.

The investigation was conducted by Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) Tulsa with assistance from the Tulsa County Election Board. Assistant U.S. Attorney Augustus Forster is prosecuting the case.

A criminal complaint is merely an allegation. The defendant is presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

The public plays a critical role in maintaining election security. Anyone who witnesses or has direct knowledge of potential election fraud, voter intimidation, or unlawful voting activity is strongly encouraged to report it immediately.

Please visit the official FBI Tips Portal or contact local law enforcement to report potential election fraud or voting irregularities. Complaints regarding voter discrimination or civil rights violations can also be directed to the Civil Rights Division via the Department of Justice Civil Rights Reporting Portal .
title: Philippine National Charged with Voting Illegally as an Alien in Federal Election

H Block Gang Member Pleads Guilty To Drug Conspiracy
BOSTON – A member of the violent Boston-based gang, H-Block, has pleaded guilty in federal court in Boston to drug conspiracy charges.
Robert Heckstall, a/k/a “Ribbs,” a/k/a “Buck,” a/k/a “Buck Corleone,” 43, of Roxbury, pleaded guilty on to conspiracy to distribute and to possess with intent to distribute PCP, MDMB-4en-PINACA and ADB-4en-PINACA; being a felon in possession of a firearm and ammunition; and possession with intent to distribute cocaine. U.S. District Court Judge Indira Talwani scheduled sentencing for Jan. 26, 2027.
Heckstall was one of 10 H-Block gang members and associates charged in August 2024 following a multi-year investigation of H-Block beginning in 2021 in response to an uptick in gang-related drug trafficking, shootings and violence. Over 500 grams of cocaine, cocaine base (crack cocaine) and fentanyl, as well as over 20,000 doses of drug-laced paper were seized during the investigation.
According to the charging documents, the H-Block street gang is one of the most feared and influential city-wide gangs in Boston. Originally formed in the 1980s as the Humboldt Raiders in the Roxbury section of Boston, the gang re-emerged in the 2000s as H-Block. Current members of H-Block have a history of violent confrontation with law enforcement, including an incident in 2015 when a member shot a Boston Police officer at point blank range without warning or provocation.
Heckstall was a long-time H-Block gang member and one of three members and associates charged with conspiring to smuggle illegal drugs into a Massachusetts prison. According to court documents, the Massachusetts Department of Correction has seen a significant increase in the smuggling of synthetic cannabinoids, a/k/a “K2,” and other dangerous substances into the prison system. A common method of introducing the drugs is by exploiting the Department of Correction’s inmate mail policies, which prohibit delivery to inmates of original copies of any materials contained in incoming mail except for legal mail, original copies of which are inspected and delivered via the U.S. postal system. Sheets of paper are saturated or sprayed with liquid narcotics, dried, printed with fake legal correspondence, and then mailed to inmates in an envelope marked as legal mail, in the hope that the drug-laced paper will be delivered undetected. Several sheets of paper containing PCP (Phenylcyclidine) and illegal K2 were seized over the course of the investigation. It is estimated that a single sheet of such paper would be worth as much as $80,000 inside the prison. Intercepted jail calls revealed that Heckstall along with his co-conspirators, conspired to introduce synthetic drugs into the facilities. When Heckstall was arrested, investigators discovered three firearms and over 60 grams of cocaine in his apartment.
Heckstall is the nineth defendant to plead guilty in the case.
The charges of conspiracy to distribute and to possess with intent to distribute PCP, MDMB-4en-PINACA and ADB-4en-PINACA and possession with intent to distribute cocaine provides for a sentence of up to 20 years in prison, at least three years and up to a lifetime of supervised release and a fine of up to $1 million. The charge of being a felon in possession of a firearm and ammunition provides for a sentence of up to 15 years in prison, supervised release for 3 years and a fine of up to $250,000. Sentences are imposed by a federal district court judge based upon the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and statutes which govern the determination of a sentence in a criminal case.
United States Attorney Leah B. Foley; Jarod A. Forget, Special Agent in Charge of the Drug Enforcement Administration, New England Field Division; Special Agent in Charge Mark Comorosky of the U.S. Secret Service Boston Field Office; Ted. E. Docks, Special Agent in Charge of the Federal Bureau of Investigation, Boston Division; Kelly M. Lawson, Special Agent in Charge of the Depart of Labor, Office of Inspector General; and Boston Police Commissioner Michael Cox made the announcement. The investigation was supported by the Massachusetts State Police; Suffolk County District Attorney’s Office; Massachusetts Department of Corrections; and the Braintree, Quincy, Randolph, and Watertown Police Departments. Assistant United States Attorney John T. Dawley of the Organized Crime & Gang Unit is prosecuting the cases.
This case is part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of United States law enforcement towards identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States. HSTF Boston comprises agents and officers from HSI, FBI, DEA, ATF, USMS, IRS-CI, USPIS, DOL-OIG and DSS, as well as several state and local law enforcement agencies, with the prosecution being led by the United States Attorney’s Office for the District of Massachusetts.
The details contained in the charging documents are allegations. The remaining defendants are presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.
title: H Block Gang Member Pleads Guilty To Drug Conspiracy

Maple leaf, meet ballot thief: ICE HSI Tucson arrests Canadian for voter fraud
TUCSON, Az. — Monique Gignac-Yochum, a lawful permanent resident from Canada, was taken into custody by ICE Homeland Security Investigations Tucson on Oct. 28 for illegally voting as an alien. Gignac-Yochum had registered to vote in the state of Wisconsin, falsely claiming U.S. citizenship, and voted in the Nov. 8, 2022, and Nov. 5, 2024, general elections. On Oct. 23, 2026, a federal misdemeanor arrest warrant was issued out of the Western District of Wisconsin for her arrest. However, Gignac-Yochum had moved to Arizona. HSI Milwaukee then reached out to HSI Tucson, leading to an arrest just days later.
"Gignac-Yochum allegedly voted illegally in not one, but two federal elections, then moved more than a thousand miles away,” said ICE Assistant Director of Public Affairs Micah Bock. “Falsely claiming U.S. citizenship to vote isn’t a paperwork mistake. It’s a serious violation of federal law that undermines public trust in our elections. Moving across state lines didn’t put her beyond the reach of federal law enforcement. If someone breaks our election laws, they should expect to be held accountable.”
This investigation reflects ICE’s continued commitment to protecting the integrity of the nation’s electoral process through coordination with federal, state and local law enforcement partners. Under President Trump, Secretary Mullin and acting ICE Director David J. Venturella’s leadership, ICE is once again focused on enforcing the law, protecting the public and removing individuals who break the law from our communities.
You can report crimes, including voter fraud, by calling 866-DHS-2-ICE (866-347-2423) or completing the online tip form. Learn more about ICE’s public safety mission on X, Facebook, Instagram, Threads, Bluesky and Truth Social.

The National Labor Relations Board (NLRB) today announced the appointment of Amy L. Cocuzza as the new Solicitor. Ms. Cocuzza is now the chief legal advisor and consultant to the entire Board on all questions of law regarding the Board’s general operations and on major questions of law and policy concerning the adjudication of NLRB cases in the Courts of Appeals and the U.S. Supreme Court. She also serves as the Board’s legal representative and liaison to the General Counsel and other offices of the Board.

Ms. Cocuzza brings to the Board more than two decades of experience in labor law, administrative law, and workplace relations. She began her legal career as an Honors Attorney for then-NLRB General Counsel Ronald Meisburg, gaining experience with various GC-side branches including Regional Advice, Appeals, and Appellate and Supreme Court Litigation, as well as the Region 5 Washington Resident Office. She went on to spend nearly a decade with the Division of Advice, rising from staff attorney to supervisory attorney before moving Board-side.

Most recently, Ms. Cocuzza was the Acting Chief of Staff to Board Chairman James R. Murphy. Prior to that, she served as Deputy Solicitor to former Solicitor Fred B. Jacob, who recently became Chief Counsel to Board Member David M. Prouty.

“With her years of experience at the NLRB and in the Solicitor’s Office, Amy will bring legal prowess, institutional wisdom, and diplomatic savvy to her new position as the Board’s Chief Legal Advisor,” said former Solicitor Fred Jacob. “Amy is committed to the NLRB’s mission and the public we serve. The Board is lucky to have her.”

Board Chairman James Murphy notes: “Former Solicitor Fred Jacob set a high standard for excellence in the performance of his duties in that office. We are very fortunate to have someone like Amy Cocuzza as a successor so worthy and qualified to uphold that standard.”

Board Member Dave Prouty remarked: “Amy Cocuzza is the right person at the right time to take on this tremendously important job at the Board. I look forward to relying on her wise counsel as “The Board’s Lawyer” for many years to come.”

Ms. Cocuzza received her B.S. in Human Biology from the University at Albany (SUNY), her Master of Industrial and Labor Relations from Cornell University, and her J.D. from the University of Michigan Law School, where she served as Editor-in-Chief of the University of Michigan Journal of Law Reform. Prior to attending law school, Ms. Cocuzza spent several years organizing with labor unions in New York City, representing healthcare workers with 1199 SEIU and professional musicians with Local 802, American Federation of Musicians. She has also taught labor law at the Antonin Scalia Law School of George Mason University.

Established in 1935, the National Labor Relations Board is an independent federal agency that protects employees from unfair labor practices and protects the right of private sector employees to join together, with or without a union, to improve wages, benefits and working conditions. The NLRB conducts hundreds of workplace elections and investigates thousands of unfair labor practice charges each year.
title: Amy L. Cocuzza Named Solicitor to the National Labor Relations Board

Oregon Delegation Celebrates Federal Support for Oregon’s Hazelnut, Seafood Industries
Washington, D.C. – Today, Oregon’s U.S. Senator Jeff Merkley led Oregon Congressional Delegation members—including Senator Ron Wyden and U.S. Representatives Suzanne Bonamici (OR-01), Val Hoyle (OR-04), Andrea Salinas (OR-06), Maxine Dexter (OR-03), and Janelle Bynum (OR-05)—to announce that after pressure from the delegation, the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) will purchase hazelnuts and Pacific Whiting fillets under the agency’s Section 32 purchase program. These purchases will benefit communities and rural economies across Oregon by supporting domestic production and distribution of these agricultural goods during periods of significant market disruption and economic uncertainty.
“Our fisheries and farms deliver incredible products all around the world and are the lifeblood of our communities,” said Merkley, who led the Oregon delegation in pressing USDA to include hazelnuts and whiting in its latest food purchase. “This announcement ensures Oregon’s harvesters, processors, and producers will receive critical financial assistance needed to continue operating and providing services here in Oregon and beyond. I am elated the USDA has decided to make these purchases—this is a win for communities across our state.”
“Iconic state industries like agriculture and fishing count on the U.S. Department of Agriculture to do its job and support Oregonians working hard to keep producing their world-class goods,” said Wyden. “I’m glad the full-court press from the delegation has unlocked this win for Oregonians fishing Pacific whiting and growing hazelnuts.”
“Oregonians know that hazelnuts and seafood are some of the state’s most popular and delicious products,” said Bonamici. “Our growers and producers work tirelessly and bolster the local economy. I’m glad the USDA is making this investment.”
“These investments from the USDA will support the people who harvest, process and bring Pacific Whiting fish and hazelnuts to market,” said Hoyle. “By putting Oregon fishermen and farmers first, we’re boosting our coastal and rural economies."
“Oregon’s specialty crop growers are the backbone of our economy, but too many are struggling with rising costs and uncertain markets,” said Salinas. “In the Willamette Valley, generations of farmers have depended on the hazelnut industry for their livelihoods. That’s why I joined my colleagues in pushing USDA to purchase Oregon hazelnuts and Pacific whiting. These purchases will provide much-needed support for our growers and fishing communities while putting more Oregon-grown and Oregon-caught food onto kitchen tables. I’m proud we secured this win for Oregon producers, and I’ll keep fighting to make sure our specialty crop farmers have the markets and resources they need to succeed.”
"Oregon’s farmers and fishermen work hard to feed our communities, and they deserve a federal government that stands behind them,” said Dexter. “Our delegation pushed USDA to act, and these $34 million in purchases will support Oregon’s hazelnut growers and fishermen during a difficult economic stretch. This investment will help sustain local jobs, strengthen rural and coastal economies, and get nutritious food to families who need it.”
“Our farmers are putting in the work every day to keep Oregon families fed,” said Bynum. “And they’re not just helping put food on the table, they’re keeping money with our families, creating good jobs close to home, and giving people what they need to put down roots here in Oregon. Money back in our state and with our farmers is a win-win.”
Previously, Merkley and the Oregon delegation pressed the USDA to include Pacific whiting and Oregon hazelnuts, which account for 99 percent of hazelnuts produced in the United States, in this year’s Section 32 purchases. Following their efforts, the USDA announced it was purchasing $22 million in hazelnuts and $12 million in Pacific whiting.
title: Oregon Delegation Celebrates Federal Support for Oregon’s Hazelnut, Seafood Industries

Tallahassee, Florida – Lekishaann Huggins, 45, of Tallahassee, Florida, pleaded guilty in federal court to 39 counts of bank fraud, one count of aggravated identity theft, and four counts of spending money laundering. This investigation is a part of the Task Force to Eliminate Fraud launched by President Donald J. Trump, a whole-of-government effort to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs. John P. Heekin, United States Attorney for the Northern District of Florida, announced the charges today.

U.S. Attorney Heekin said: “This fraudster pocketed federal funds intended to provide housing assistance to low-income citizens to instead throw herself a lavish holiday party and purchase jewelry, designer purses, and other luxury items using your taxpayer dollars. This is beyond despicable, but thanks to the leadership of President Donald J. Trump, the Task Force to Eliminate Fraud and DOJ’s National Fraud Enforcement Division are striking back against the fraudsters who have ripped off the American taxpayer.”

Court documents reveal that in 2023 and 2024, the defendant was employed as a Housing Choice Voucher Manager for the Tallahassee Housing Authority (THA). The investigation revealed the defendant embezzled 40 payments totaling approximately $378,927. She accomplished this by using the names and profiles of 16 former THA tenants. The defendant falsely billed non-existent rent payments to a company she controlled. In January 2025, THA, who received and administered federal funds provided by the United States Department of Housing and Urban Development, notified law enforcement of suspicious entries in their tracking systems. Law enforcement’s investigation revealed the defendant also filed false tax returns in 2023 and 2024 involving her stated income and falsifying forms. As part of her plea, the defendant agreed to forfeit jewelry, clothing, and accessories seized during the investigation.

The defendant faces up to 30 years’ imprisonment for each of the 39 counts of bank fraud, 2 years’ imprisonment consecutive to any other imprisonment for the aggravated identity theft count, up to 10 years’ imprisonment for each spending money laundering count, restitution, and forfeiture of assets.

Sentencing is scheduled for January 12, 2027, at 10:30 am at the United States Courthouse in Tallahassee, Florida before Chief United States District Judge Allen C. Winsor.

On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the National Fraud Enforcement Division (“Fraud Division”). The Fraud Division is investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.

The case was investigated by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, Office of Inspector General and the Internal Revenue Service-Criminal Investigations with assistance from the Tallahassee Police Department and the Leon County Sheriff’s Office. Assistant United States Attorneys Eric W. Welch and Michelle Spaven are prosecuting the case.

The United States Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Florida is one of 94 offices that serve as the nation’s principal litigators under the direction of the Attorney General. To access available public court documents online, please visit the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Florida website. For more information about the United States Attorney’s Office, Northern District of Florida, visit https://www.justice.gov/usao-ndfl .
title: Tallahassee Woman Pleads Guilty to Defrauding the Tallahassee Housing Authority

The Department of the Air Force’s Spark Tank program concludes its final year with the Top 5 ideas selected out of 350 total submissions. These ideas endured strict subject matter evaluation from 1,394 members casting nearly 26,000 votes, evaluation from command leadership, and final determination by a panel of innovation leaders.
Out of 350 total submissions from across the Air and Space Forces, the Spark Tank 2026 Top 5 are:
Automated Master Storage Plan (Air Combat Command) – Leverages artificial intelligence to plan warehouse layouts for munitions, enabling weeks of planning to be executed in minutes.
M-UAS-D, MANET-enabled UAS Detector (Air Combat Command) – Low-cost for large scale deployment, a counter sUAS to detect drones, share real-time range data to users and response teams.
Project CAPYBARA (Air Mobility Command) – A set of tutorials and parts lists provided to any organization to build custom rovers for any capability needed in the field, replacing costly TDYs and certification programs.
Secure STIG Checker (Air Force Special Operations Command) – Replaces Enterprise Network manual compliance checks with a tool capable of analyzing millions of lines of code in under 500 seconds.
Tac-Hub: Agile Communications for the Modern Mission (Air Force Global Strike Command) – Modular command and control suite to enable rapid deployment; designed for military and emergency response teams.
Spark Tank is the Department of the Air Force's premier campaign where Guardians and Airmen present their innovative solutions to top leaders and industry experts, seeking sponsorship to bring their concepts to life.
The Top 5 teams will now accelerate prototypes and forge strategic partnerships with the help of AFWERX Refinery and DAF Enterprise Innovation support.
A panel of judges also reviewed the following semi-finalist submissions, which will be migrated for support and progression:
Aerial Minefield (Air Combat Command) – Low cost solution to create dense clouds of aerial obstacles to defend against and disable low-cost adversarial drones.
Agile Cyber Training Environment: Portable Cyber Ops Center (Air Combat Command) – Portable, battery-powered, network-independent center globally deployable by a single person in less than a minute for agile cyber operations.
Contingency Remote Optical Charging Spacecraft (Space Systems Group) – Charges dead spacecraft with ground lasers to prevent abandoned spacecraft and lost satellites due to loss of power.
Energy Resilience Command Platform (Air Force Reserve Command) – Dashboard unifying all base energy, power, water, heating, and mission critical data into a real time “Base Resilience Percentage”, indicating operational sustainment during disruptions.
Flight Room 3D Models (Air Education and Training Command) – Standardizes and institutionalizes 3D printed models of pilot curriculum items.
Project HOPLITE (Air Force Special Operations Command) – Integrates key components from Land Phalanx Weapon System, tactical truck, or FMTV load handling system to create a flexible and rapidly deployable air defense solution, transportable by C-130.
(ReSearch) an Advanced Search Engine for EPubs (Air Force Material Command) – Integrates Advana’s advanced search engine, natural language processing, and data analytics into the EPubs platform to allow Airmen to find exactly what they are looking for.
SpartReg 36-2903 Pictures of Dress Right vs. Wrong (Pacific Air Forces) – Digital interactive guide with side-by-side “correct vs. incorrect” examples, hyperlinks, and visual decision trees for dress and appearance standards.
Streamline 1205 Narrative Sync (Pacific Air Forces) – Standardize Air Force writing style by switching from character count format that matches EPB/ORB narrative standards.
The Sheppard Blueprint: A Proven Model for CONUS MTF Pharmacy Recapture (Air Education and Training Command) – Low-cost and highly replicable, a text message outreach and 24/7 prescription lockers to prevent lost cost in on-base pharmacies.
Vehicle Diagnostic System (Air National Guard) – Consolidates 5 tools and 7 software licenses into 1 tool for vehicle diagnostics.
title: DAF announces Spark Tank 2026 Top 5

The National Endowment for the Humanities (NEH) is pleased to announce a special funding opportunity to strengthen the teaching of classical humanities curriculum in American high schools. The agency has issued a call for proposals for High School Classical Curriculum Chairman’s Grants, a new initiative to enhance existing programs, resources, or courses in the fields of Classics, Great Books, and Western Civilization. “NEH’s investment in classical education is an investment in the next generation of thoughtful, informed, and engaged citizens,” said NEH Chairman Michael McDonald. “The programs supported by this special opportunity will give students a grounding in the major ideas, events, and books that have shaped American society, and will equip them with the knowledge to address contemporary challenges.”
High School Classical Curriculum Chairman’s Grants will support humanities curriculum development and educational programs focused on enhancing the capacity to teach Classics, Great Books, and/or Western Civilization. Eligible proposals might include revising current or developing new courses in the above topics; developing materials to support teaching in these interest areas, such as books, curated student resources, or teaching curriculum guides; faculty development, including collaboration with local cultural institutions, neighboring schools or districts, and/or nearby institutions of higher education.
Applicants must currently teach courses in one of the following interest areas: Classics, Great Books, and/or Western Civilization. NEW ORLEANS , LOUISIANA – YEFRI ISAIS AGUIRRE-CASTRO ("AGUIRRE-CASTRO") , age 38, a national of Honduras, was indicted on October 29, 2026, for forcibly assaulting, resisting, impeding, and/or interfering with a federal officer, in violation of Title 18, United States Code, Section 111(a)(1), announced United States Attorney David I. Courcelle.

According to the indictment, on October 22, 2026, AGUIRRE-CASTRO , forcibly assaulted, resisted, impeded, and/or interfered with, through physical contact, a Department of Homeland Security, Customs and Border Patrol Supervisory Agent while the agent was engaged in the performance of his official duties.

If convicted, AGUIRRE-CASTRO faces up to eight (8) years in prison, up to a $250,000 fine, and up to three (3) years of supervised release. The indictment also carries a mandatory $100 special assessment fee.

U.S. Attorney David I. Courcelle reiterated that the indictment is merely an allegation and that the guilt of the defendant must be proven beyond a reasonable doubt.

The case was investigated by the Department of Homeland Security, Customs and Border Patrol. The U.S. Attorney’s Office also praises the hard work of the Slidell Police Department and the St. Tammany Parish Sheriff’s Office. Assistant United States Attorneys Spiro G. Latsis and Connor Crowley of the General Crimes Unit are in charge of the prosecution.

This case is part of Operation Take Back America a nationwide initiative that marshals the full resources of the Department of Justice to repel the invasion of illegal immigration, achieve the total elimination of cartels and transnational criminal organizations (TCOs), and protect our communities from the perpetrators of violent crime.

OPM Review Identifies $106.7 Million in Improper Payments in FEHBP
WASHINGTON, DC – The US Office of Personnel Management (OPM) has identified approximately 50,000 deceased individuals who remain listed in the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program (FEHBP) by matching Treasury’s August 2026 Death Record Confidence Scoring Tool (DRCST) against OPM’s FEHB enrollment records.
The review identified $96.3 million in improper payments made after date of death, including $70.6 million in government FEHB premium contributions and $25.7 million in retirement payments.
OPM also estimates $10.4 million in carrier costs tied to over 20,000 individuals who remain on carrier rolls even though no government premium is being paid for them. Carriers charge FEHB funds each month for administrative and per-member costs. OPM will examine claims that may have been paid after date of death in the coming weeks.
“Every outdated enrollment record can carry a cost. This review is helping us find those records, identify payments that need action, and reduce unnecessary costs to FEHB,” OPM Associate Director of Healthcare and Insurance Matthew Kiley said.
“We will not allow the taxpayer to shoulder the burden of fraud, waste, or improper payments. These findings are a drop in the bucket of what we expect to find as we double down on our integrity program,” OPM Director Scott Kupor said.
“Here is a simple rule only President Trump and Vice President Vance understand: Dead people should not receive health benefits. Today is another critical step forward in reversing the errors by the previous administration,” Executive Director of the White House Task Force to Eliminate Fraud Scott Bradysaid.
title: OPM Review Identifies $106.7 Million in Improper Payments in FEHBP

In a strategic effort to outpace adversaries and accelerate the adoption of cutting-edge technology, the U.S. Army is inviting private industry to test their systems against realistic battlefield conditions. As a key component of the Army's broader Permissive Test Range Initiative, a series of electromagnetic unreliability test events are providing commercial vendors with unique, dedicated opportunities to strengthen their drone, counter-drone, long-range fires and low-cost interceptor technologies in contested electronic warfare environments.
Launched in August 2026, the Permissive Test Range Initiative aims to remove bureaucratic hurdles for private companies, granting them streamlined access to premier military test and training ranges. Spearheaded by the U.S. Army Test and Evaluation Command (ATEC), the goal is to create a space where companies can conduct their own internal research, development and rapid innovation on large spaces that may not be available in the commercial sector.
The electromagnetic unreliability test events are a focused element of this initiative, created in partnership with the U.S. Army's Threat Systems Management Office (TSMO). These events are designed to replicate the challenging electronic warfare environments that U.S. forces and their allies face today. By subjecting systems to denied, degraded, intermittent and limited electromagnetic spectrum conditions, the Army is giving developers a rare chance to see how their platforms perform when GPS signals are denied or communication links are jammed.
"By opening our premier test facilities and providing access to realistic threat environments, we are directly enabling industry to refine their systems against the challenges of the modern battlefield," said Maj. Gen. Pat Gaydon, commanding general of ATEC. "These electromagnetic unreliability events are about accelerating the delivery of resilient, effective and reliable capabilities to our Soldiers. We are creating the conditions for industry to innovate at the speed of relevance, ensuring our warfighters maintain their technological edge."
Camp Grayling launch
The inaugural event was held at Camp Grayling, Michigan, in September 2026, where four drone companies participated. The feedback from these vendors was overwhelmingly positive. A common theme was a deep appreciation for the opportunity to identify critical vulnerabilities and mature their system capabilities in real-time. This "fly, fail, fix, fly again" methodology, conducted in a non-competitive environment free from government evaluation or down-selects, proved invaluable for hardening their systems.
"Camp Grayling gives the Department of War and its industry partners the ability to put emerging technologies in an environment that mirrors the challenges our forces could encounter in a contested fight,” said Col. Lucas Lanczy, commander of Camp Grayling Joint Maneuver Training Center. “Our combination of expansive training areas, diverse terrain, electromagnetic spectrum access and multi-domain capabilities allows innovators and military organizations to test systems under realistic conditions, identify gaps and rapidly improve them. This is exactly the kind of experimentation that helps ensure technology is in the hands of our Warfighters when they need it.”
Looking ahead
Building on the success of the first event, the Army has scheduled three more large-scale events for 2027:
- Feb. 1-5 at Dugway Proving Ground, Utah
- June 14-18 at West Cibola Range, part of Yuma Proving Ground, Arizona
- Sept. 20-24 at Camp Shelby, Mississippi
The upcoming event at Dugway Proving Ground will expand the scope of testing, offering vendors the chance to not only conduct drone and counter-drone experimentation in a contested electromagnetic environment, but also to experiment with long-range fires and low-cost interceptors. These capabilities were not included in the Camp Grayling event.
Companies interested in participating can submit a request through the U.S. Army Test Range Portal, testrange.army.mil, where a dedicated government concierge will guide them through the scheduling process. This initiative marks a significant shift in how the Army collaborates with the commercial sector to ensure the nation's military is equipped with the most resilient and advanced technology possible.
title: Army electromagnetic unreliability events empower industry to test drone, fires resilience

SPRINGFIELD, MA— Ways and Means Committee Ranking Member Richard E. Neal (D-MA) released the following statement after President Trump announced intention to terminate South Africa from the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) trade preference program:
“For 26 years, AGOA has been the cornerstone of a profound economic partnership between the U.S. and sub-Saharan African countries. Together, we’ve expanded trade, promoted job creation and worker rights, and strengthened democratic institutions. For the Trump Administration to abandon South Africa and strip them of that progress and opportunity over a debunked fixation on anti-apartheid efforts is unconscionable. It’s yet another trade decision grounded in grievance that flies in the face of what responsible policy should be.
“The Administration owes the American people a more thorough explanation as to why South Africa was removed from AGOA and what steps South Africa can take to be reinstated to the program. Livelihoods, businesses, and U.S. credibility are on the line. The power of our trade laws shouldn’t be twisted so Trump can further policies based on biased accusations made by those in his orbit looking to settle scores. The last thing our trade policy needs, and families and businesses at home can afford, is more Trump chaos that shakes our economy, puts investment at risk, and erodes America’s standing on the continent.”
###
