Thirty Armed Services Democrats, Veterans, Raise Alarm Over March Attack on NSA Bahrain, Pentagon’s Poor Treatment of Evacuated Military Families
Congressmembers Deluzio, Ryan, and Senator Blumenthal led the letter to Secretary Hegseth, letter covered by MSNOW
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, 30 members of Congress signed on to a letter demanding action and answers from the Pentagon about the poor treatment of military servicemembers and their families who were evacuated from Naval Support Activity Bahrain (NSA Bahrain) in March 2026.
This letter comes after MS NOW reported on the details of a hasty and traumatic evacuation from NSA Bahrain in March, noting that many military family members have been living out of hotels and short-term rentals and are being required to pay out of pocket to cover these expenses. The letter demands that the Department of Defense right this wrong and support these evacuated military families.
The members of Congress also asked the Secretary how much it would cost to repair the severe damage to NSA Bahrain and how the incapacitation of the base has impacted U.S. operations in the Iran War and the wider Middle East.
The letter is co-led by Congressman Chris Deluzio (PA-17), Congressman Pat Ryan (NY-18), and Senator Richard Blumenthal (CT). The letter signatories are members of the House Armed Services Committee, the Senate Armed Services Committee, or are members of the Democratic Veterans Caucus.
The letter reads, “President Trump launched the Iran War on February 28th before evacuating the roughly 8,300 military personnel, DoD civilians, and their families stationed at NSA Bahrain. Families were authorized to evacuate only after the war started, subjecting them to the Iranian retaliatory strikes that heavily damaged the base. Since March, these evacuees have been under constant emotional, financial, and psychological stress... While the Department of Defense has provided safe haven entitlements to offset the cost of living for evacuees, this funding is scheduled to be terminated in November or after the 180th day of receiving the entitlement, before many have found permanent housing and transportation.”
The members continue, “Because NSA Bahrain was a critical logistics hub for U.S. Central Command, we require a better understanding of how the severe damage to the base has impacted U.S. operations… We have significant concerns about the morale and welfare of the troops deployed to the region, especially in light of the reporting on the conditions onboard the USS Gerald R. Ford and USS Abraham Lincoln, which both served record breaking deployments.”
Specifically, the members requested answers by November 13, 2026 to the following questions:
- Why was the Navy’s request to extend the safe haven entitlements for evacuees denied?
  - Who made this decision?
- Why are safe haven entitlements for evacuees being terminated before the arrival of household goods?
- What will the Department of Defense do to ensure that evacuees from NSA Bahrain are not paying out of pocket for living expenses incurred by the evacuation?
  - What processes, if any, are in place for evacuees to receive reimbursement for expenses incurred, and how many reimbursement cases are pending?
- Given the damage to NSA Bahrain, which logistic hub (or hubs) has the Department of Defense been using amidst the Iran War?
- What has been the operational impact of the loss of NSA Bahrain?
- Does the Department of Defense intend to repair and rebuild NSA Bahrain?
  - If so, how much is the expected cost for such work?
  - What is the financial cost of the damage to NSA Bahrain?
The House signatories of the letter are: Reps. Chris Deluzio (PA-17, co-lead), Pat Ryan (NY-18, co-lead), Wesley Bell (MO-01), Salud Carbajal (CA-24), Gil Cisneros (CA-31), Herb Conaway (NJ-03), Joe Courtney (CT-02), Jason Crow (CO-06), Sarah Elfreth (MD-03), John Garamendi (CA-08), Maggie Goodlander (NH-02), Chrissy Houlahan (PA-06), Sara Jacobs (CA-51), Bill Keating (MA-09), Ro Khanna (CA-17), Ted Lieu (CA-36), Jimmy Panetta (CA-19), Adam Smith (WA-09), Eric Sorensen (IL-17), Marilyn Strickland (WA-10), Mike Thompson (CA-04), Derek Tran (CA-45), Eugene Vindman (VA-07), and George Whitesides (CA-27).
The Senate signatories of the letter are: Sens. Richard Blumenthal (CT, co-lead), Tammy Duckworth (IL), Kirstin Gillibrand (NY), Mazie Hirono (HI), Jacky Rosen (NV), Elizabeth Warren (MA).
The full text of the letter is below and is linked here.
Dear Secretary Hegseth:
We write to raise concern over reporting that servicemembers and their families are continuing to face significant hardship following their evacuation from Naval Support Activity Bahrain (NSA Bahrain) in March this year. Additionally, we seek to better understand how the incapacitation of NSA Bahrain has impacted U.S. operations in the Iran War and the broader Middle East. In an August town hall, Chief of Naval Operations, Adm. Daryl Caudle, said that the Navy would not be using NSA Bahrain for the foreseeable future. This is significant not only for the thousands of servicemembers and their families personally involved, but also because NSA Bahrain is a critical logistics hub that has served as the headquarters for U.S. Naval Forces Central Command and U.S. Navy Fifth Fleet since 1995.
Servicemembers and Their Families are Not Receiving Adequate Support
As you know, President Trump launched the Iran War on February 28th before evacuating the roughly 8,300 military personnel, DoD civilians, and their families stationed at NSA Bahrain. Families were authorized to evacuate only after the war started, subjecting them to the Iranian retaliatory strikes that heavily damaged the base. Since March, these evacuees have been under constant emotional, financial, and psychological stress. Some have had to move across continents, stay in temporary lodging for months, enroll their children in a new school mid-year, pay out of pocket for significant costs associated with a move and more, all often without access to belongings they were forced to leave behind. While the Department of Defense has provided safe haven entitlements to offset the cost of living for evacuees, this funding is scheduled to be terminated in November or after the 180th day of receiving the entitlement, before many have found permanent housing and transportation.
In a recent town hall, Navy officials relayed that your Department of Defense leadership had denied a request to extend the safe haven entitlements, and that each evacuee had to seek individual approval from the Acting Secretary of the Navy. This is unacceptable. To make matters worse, the signing of a lease is being used as a triggering event for termination of the safe haven entitlement. This is bad policy. Although a family may have signed a lease for a permanent residence, they may still have to use a rental vehicle or stay in temporary lodging while they wait for their household goods to arrive from overseas. Requiring servicemembers to pay out of pocket for expenses that were forced upon them by your mismanagement of the Iran War is wrong. You must fix this.
Loss of NSA Bahrain and U.S. Presence in the Middle East
As the Iran War reaches the ninth month, our constituents have expressed increasing concern about the cost of the conflict and the lack of transparency surrounding U.S. operations and strategic goals in the region. Because NSA Bahrain was a critical logistics hub for U.S. Central Command, we require a better understanding of how the severe damage to the base has impacted U.S. operations. In August, the New York Times reported that the U.S Navy is now resupplying from Diego Garcia, an island in the Indian Ocean 2,200 miles away from the Persian Gulf. We have significant concerns about the morale and welfare of the troops deployed to the region, especially in light of the reporting on the conditions onboard the USS Gerald R. Ford and USS Abraham Lincoln, which both served record breaking deployments.
In executing the Congress’s oversight authority under Article I of the Constitution, we request answers to the following questions by November 13, 2026. 
- Why was the Navy’s request to extend the safe haven entitlements for evacuees denied?
  - Who made this decision?
- Why are safe haven entitlements for evacuees being terminated before the arrival of household goods?
- What will the Department of Defense do to ensure that evacuees from NSA Bahrain are not paying out of pocket for living expenses incurred by the evacuation? 
  - What processes, if any, are in place for evacuees to receive reimbursement for expenses incurred, and how many reimbursement cases are pending?
- Given the damage to NSA Bahrain, which logistic hub (or hubs) has the Department of Defense been using amidst the Iran War?
- What has been the operational impact of the loss of NSA Bahrain?
- Does the Department of Defense intend to repair and rebuild NSA Bahrain? 
  - If so, how much is the expected cost for such work?
  - What is the financial cost of the damage to NSA Bahrain?
###

CHARLOTTE, N.C. – U.S. Attorney Russ Ferguson announced today that Assistant U.S. Attorney (AUSA) Alex M. Scott and Appellate Paralegal Linda Cole were selected as recipients of the 2026 Executive Office for United States Attorneys (EOUSA) Director’s Award. AUSA Alex M. Scott received the Director’s Award for Superior Performance in Indian Country, and Appellate Paralegal Linda Cole received the Lifetime Exceptional Service Award for her decades of service in the Office’s Appellate Division. The Director’s Award recognizes excellence across the U.S. Attorney community and honors the exceptional contributions to the Justice Department’s mission by attorneys and support personnel, serving in the nation’s 94 federal districts.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Alex M. Scott

AUSA Alex M. Scott joined the U.S. Attorney’s Office in Asheville in 2022, where he leads complex prosecutions involving drug trafficking, firearms, and violent crime, among others. As the Western District’s Tribal Liaison, AUSA Scott serves as the lead prosecutor in cases arising on the Qualla Boundary, home of the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians (EBCI), and on the federally recognized trust land of the Catawba Nation in North Carolina. Notably, as part of the Justice Department’s Missing and Murdered Indigenous Persons (MMIP) initiative, AUSA Scott prosecuted U.S. v. Ernest Pheasant , securing a life sentence for the 2013 murder of Marie Walkingstick Pheasant, resolving a long-standing cold case in Indian Country.

AUSA Scott began his career in public service as an Assistant District Attorney in Johnson County, Kansas, from 2013 to 2021. He joined the United States Attorney’s Office in Tulsa, Oklahoma in 2021, where he prosecuted violent crime offenses in Indian Country. AUSA Scott received his Bachelor of Science degree from the University of Missouri in 2009, and his J.D. with honors from the University of Missouri – Kansas City School of Law in 2012.

“Alex is a stellar example of the best the Justice Department has to offer,” said U.S. Attorney Russ Ferguson. “The Justice Department has recognized his exceptional legal advocacy and trial skills, which have helped make North Carolina communities safer. Alex is also an outstanding representative of the Justice Department in Indian Country. As a relationship-builder and a committed advocate for victims, Alex delivers justice while respecting the sovereignty and laws of the EBCI and the Catawba Nation.”

Appellate Paralegal Linda Cole

Linda Cole has been a public servant for 50 years, including more than 44 years of distinguished service to the Department of Justice and the U.S. Attorney’s Office in Asheville. As a paralegal in the Appellate Division, Linda has been responsible for docketing and tracking thousands of appeals and post-conviction matters, drafting and editing legal documents, and generating accurate statistics and reports for the Appellate Division. Linda maintains a comprehensive database of deadlines and provides reminders to Appellate AUSAs to ensure that no filing or deadline is ever missed. Linda approaches all aspects of her work with efficiency, professionalism, and dedication to the Justice Department’s Mission.

“Linda personifies public service,” said U.S. Attorney Russ Ferguson. “She consistently goes above and beyond the call of duty to ensure our Office meets our deadlines and obligations to the Court of Appeals, and that our filings reflect the highest standards of accuracy and professionalism. Linda has devoted decades of service to the mission of the Justice Department and the people of the Western District of North Carolina and continues to serve as an example and a mentor to our newer employees.”

To learn more about the U.S. Attorney’s Office please visit our website . For employment opportunities with the U.S. Attorney’s Office in the Western District of North Carolina please go to USAJobs.gov .

LITTLE ROCK—A federal jury has convicted Renford Stephenson Williams of being a felon in possession of firearms and ammunition and possession of a machinegun. The trial, which spanned three days, ended on Thursday, October 29, 2026, with guilty verdicts on all counts for Williams, 36, of Jacksonville. Jonathan D. Ross, United States Attorney for the Eastern District of Arkansas, announced the verdict.

Williams was indicted by a federal grand jury on May 9, 2024, and ultimately went to trial on one count of being a felon in possession of firearms and ammunition and one count of possession of a machinegun.

The evidence at trial proved that Williams, who is a felon and on parole, lived at a residence in Beebe without consent from his parole officer. In June 2024, a search warrant was executed at the Beebe residence, and officers located 13 firearms in Williams’ bedroom. Also located in Williams’ bedroom were his identification card, a utility bill in his name for that Beebe address, and other documents in his name.

One of the firearms located was a Glock that was outfitted with a machinegun conversion device, making it a machinegun. Back in March 2024, Williams was a suspect in a shooting at a residence. The Arkansas State Crime Laboratory compared the 9 mm expended cartridge casings that were collected from that scene in March 2024 to all the 9 mm firearms recovered from Williams’ bedroom during the execution of the search warrant in June 2024. Analysts determined that one of the firearms, a Tisas Zigana, was used to shoot some of the 9 mm cartridge casings recovered from the scene of the shooting in March.

After deliberating for less than an hour, the jury found Williams guilty of being a felon in possession of firearms and ammunition and possession of a machinegun. Williams was detained following the jury’s verdict and will be sentenced at a later date. Williams’ charges carry a sentence of up to 15 years’ imprisonment for the felon in possession of a firearm charge, and up to 10 years’ imprisonment on the machinegun charge. Bonamici, Wyden, Merkley Demand Investigation into ICE Tire Slashing Incident
WASHINGTON, DC [11/2/26] – Today Congresswoman Suzanne Bonamici (OR-01) and Senators Ron Wyden and Jeff Merkley demanded an investigation into Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents for slashing a couple’s tires in Hillsboro.
The couple was observing and recording ICE agents in a supermarket parking lot on October 7, 2026, before multiple masked ICE agents in three vehicles tailed the couple, boxed them in, and repeatedly stabbed and slashed their tires before driving away. A video of the incident can be viewed here.
“ICE agents cannot act with impunity,” the lawmakers wrote. “The First Amendment protects the right to observe, gather information, and record law enforcement officers performing their duties in public. These constitutional protections are necessary for the public to learn about and freely debate the government’s actions, including potential misconduct, and demand accountability when necessary.”
The lawmakers noted that there have been many documented cases of excessive use of force and intimidation tactics against peaceful community members and legal observers by ICE in Oregon and across the country. They called for the Inspector General for the Department of Homeland Security to immediately investigate the Oct. 7 incident in Hillsboro, identify the agents involved, and preserve all evidence, so that those responsible may be disciplined.
“Without videos from bystanders, observers, journalists, and protestors, the public would never know the full scale of federal retaliation against those who seek to document ICE activity,” the lawmakers wrote.
Bonamici, Wyden, Merkley, and Dexter also recently raised concerns about the lack of access to counsel for individuals detained by ICE and what appear to be new protocols for bypassing the Portland ICE facility entirely. That letter can be found here.
The full letter about the Oct. 7 incident can be read here and below:
Dear Inspector General Cuffari:
We write to request an investigation into an alarming incident that occurred on October 7, 2026, in which U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents harassed, intimidated, and retaliated against a couple in Hillsboro, Oregon for engaging in First Amendment activities. The incident occurred when our constituents observed and recorded ICE agents in a supermarket parking lot. Soon thereafter, multiple masked ICE agents in three vehicles recklessly tailed the couple, boxed them in, and dangerously vandalized their vehicle by repeatedly stabbing and puncturing one of their tires before driving away.1
ICE agents cannot act with impunity. The First Amendment protects the right to observe, gather information about, and record law enforcement officers performing their duties in public.2 These constitutional protections are necessary for the public to learn about and freely debate the government’s actions, including potential misconduct, and demand accountability when necessary.
Since President Trump returned to office in January 2025, federal ICE agents across the country have repeatedly failed to respect rights afforded under the Constitution, especially the First Amendment. We have seen many documented cases of excessive use of force and intimidation tactics by ICE in Oregon, including federal agents needlessly deploying tear-gas and other projectiles against peaceful community members as well as driving erratically and verbally threatening legal observers. This pattern of irresponsible and illegal behavior from federal agents is also evident across the country. For example, federal agents in Memphis, Tennessee harassed observers by swerving at them, tailing them, boxing them in, and pulling them over without reasonable suspicion; sitting outside of their homes; and assaulting and arresting them.3 In Los Angeles, federal agents fired crowd control weapons into the heads and other sensitive areas of observers, journalists, and protestors. A judge later granted an injunction against this behavior4 and found that the plaintiffs have plausibly alleged that DHS had a policy of retaliating against people who record the activities of agents.5
Most troubling, federal immigration agents killed Alex Pretti while he was peacefully recording and protesting ICE’s actions.6 Through all of this, the Trump administration has repeatedly covered up officer misconduct and obstructed investigations.7 To this day, there is no evidence that the federal government has meaningfully investigated Mr. Pretti’s killing, with his parents noting that “at every turn, they have ignored us, misled us and shielded Alex’s killers.”8 This reckless behavior and senseless violence endangers everyone across the country and does not advance ICE’s mission of enforcing immigration laws to preserve national security and public safety.
Without videos from bystanders, observers, journalists, and protestors, the public would never know the full scale of federal retaliation against those who seek to document ICE activity.
We hereby demand that your offices immediately undertake an investigation of the October 7, 2026, incident in Hillsboro, Oregon outlined above. Please identify the ICE agents involved and preserve all relevant evidence so the officers can be disciplined and prosecuted as appropriate.
Further, we request that you undertake a comprehensive investigation of the pervasive pattern of ICE agents acting unlawfully and retaliating against individuals exercising their First Amendment rights. We ask that you work with Congress to make lasting changes to ICE training, oversight, and accountability. The rights of our constituents must not be jeopardized any longer.
Sincerely,
###
title: Bonamici, Wyden, Merkley Demand Investigation into ICE Tire Slashing Incident

VICENZA, Italy – California National Guard members worked alongside Armed Forces of Nigeria partners during an engagement in Abuja, Nigeria, Aug. 15-22, integrating the California Military Department into the AFN's ongoing air-to-ground integration efforts.
By directly addressing AGI integration, this collaboration made substantial progress on the California Guard’s top priority with Nigeria, its partner in the National Guard’s State Partnership Program since 2006.
The primary objectives of this meeting involved assessing current capability gaps in integrating Nigeria’s joint terminal attack controllers — commonly referred to as “JTACs” — into combat operations, analyzing existing force generation and training pipelines, and developing a mutually beneficial, long-term partnership roadmap, as well as future training pathways.
JTACs operate on front lines in wartime scenarios, directing combat aircraft to provide close-air support and other offensive air operations. This collaborative event was a significant step forward in strengthening interoperability between the California Guard and the AFN.
“The engagement built working relationships among the California Guard, U.S. Embassy Abuja, the Nigerian military’s Air Warfare and Doctrine Centre, and Nigerian Air Force personnel while establishing shared training priorities,” said U.S. Air Force Lt. Col. Daniel Kempf, commander of the 146th Logistics Readiness Squadron, 146th Airlift Wing, California Air National Guard. “We also set conditions for joint curriculum development, virtual instruction, in-person training and evaluator development, which will pave the way for further development and engagements,” Kempf said.
Nigeria’s Air Warfare and Doctrine Centre is the primary training institution responsible for certifying JTACs across its military. Once certified, the controllers report to active theater commands to support tactical operations. The AWDC oversees the standardization of training and continuous evaluation of its graduates, while also ensuring that those graduates maintain their skills.
“Working together, we identified JTAC training, sustainment and ground-force integration gaps, and we produced a roadmap for building a more capable, sustainable program,” Kempf said. “That program will also support safer operations and stronger civilian-harm mitigation, improving the AFN’s abilities as a regional security provider and a partner to the California National Guard.”
According to Kempf, the AFN intends to train and maintain a mission-appropriate level of certified JTACs for each of its active combat theaters to ensure a healthy operational rotation, while lowering risks faced by friendly forces and local populations. As of August 2026, the AWDC graduated two training cohorts toward meeting this long-term goal.
“While the California State Partnership Program can’t directly provide or procure operational military hardware, our capabilities are perfectly aligned to support training, curriculum development and institutional capacity building,” Kempf said. “We’ve already identified and agreed on key areas to drive long-term improvements.”
U.S. Africa Command leads “Flintlock” and “African Lion,” which are major, multinational training exercises that take place annually in Africa, focusing on improving security and cooperation with partner nations. Kempf explained that future training that further integrates the California Guard and AWDC personnel into regional exercise frameworks would involve these events, among others.
“Additional potential events include virtual ground force commander instruction, practical training in Maiduguri, Nigeria, advanced JTAC-evaluator training, as well as Nigerian JTAC and air-to-ground-integration refresher exchanges in California,” Kempf said.
Planning these training opportunities not only helps further develop working relationships between partners, they also prepare reaction forces for unexpected tasks, which can involve wartime scenarios or missions involving disaster response.
“In peacetime, we concentrate on training, doctrine, airspace management and civilian-harm mitigation,” Kempf said. “In combat or contingency operations, the focus in these engagements can improve air-to-ground coordination and reduce risks to friendly forces and civilians.”
Along with augmenting Nigerian readiness, Kempf emphasized how the engagement benefited the Golden State's warfighting trainers.
“This visit strengthened our own readiness by providing practical experience assessing a partner force’s doctrine, training pipeline, equipment limitations and security constraints,” Kempf said. “Continued engagements will provide further valuable context for the California Guard to analyze tactics, techniques and procedures currently used in active combat environments in the region.”

April Nikkel, 37, from Sioux City, Iowa, was sentenced on October 29, 2026, to 168 months’ imprisonment. Nikkel pled guilty on May 18, 2026, in federal court in Sioux City to one count of conspiracy to distribute methamphetamine and one count of distributing methamphetamine within 1,000 feet of a protected location.

Evidence at the plea and sentencing hearings showed Nikkel was involved in a conspiracy from January 2025 through November 2025 that distributed more than three pounds of methamphetamine. On at least three occasions Nikkel distributed and helped another distribute a total of over 190 grams of pure methamphetamine to individuals cooperating with law enforcement. These distributions occurred within 1,000 feet of Fairmount City Park and Cecillia City Park in Sioux City.

United States District Court Judge Leonard T. Strand sentenced Nikkel to 168 months’ imprisonment and eight years of supervised release. There is no parole in the federal system. Nikkel remains in custody of the United States Marshal until she can be transported to a federal prison.

The case was prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney Shawn S. Wehde and was investigated by Tri-State Drug Task Force based in Sioux City, Iowa, that consists of law enforcement personnel from the Drug Enforcement Administration; Sioux City, Iowa, Police Department; Homeland Security Investigations; Woodbury County Sheriff’s Office; South Sioux City, Nebraska, Police Department; Nebraska State Patrol; Iowa National Guard; Iowa Division of Narcotics Enforcement; United States Marshals Service; South Dakota Division of Criminal Investigation; and Woodbury County Attorney’s Office.

MONTGOMERY, Ala. — Today, the United States Attorney’s Office for the Middle District of Alabama, the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), the Montgomery Police Department, and the Montgomery County District Attorney’s Office announced the indictment of a Montgomery teacher on drug trafficking and firearms charges.

On October 29, 2026, a federal grand jury returned an indictment charging Langston Fremont Carter, 30, of Montgomery, Alabama, with two counts of possession of a controlled substance with intent to distribute and two additional counts related to the unlawful possession of a firearm.

According to the charging documents, the alleged offenses occurred on October 22, 2026, at L.E.A.D. Academy in Montgomery. Carter, who was employed as a teacher at the school, is accused of possessing controlled substances, including oxycodone and marijuana, with the intent to distribute them. He is also charged with possessing a firearm in furtherance of a drug trafficking crime and possessing a firearm within a school zone.

Carter made his initial appearance in federal court on October 29, 2026. His arraignment is scheduled for November 3, 2026.

If convicted on all charges, Carter faces a maximum sentence of 20 years' imprisonment on the drug trafficking charges. In addition, the charge of possessing a firearm in furtherance of a drug trafficking crime carries a mandatory minimum sentence of five years' imprisonment, which must be served consecutively to any sentence imposed on the other counts. A federal district judge will determine the sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors. There is no parole in the federal system.

The ATF and Montgomery Police Department investigated the case. Assistant U.S. Attorney Joel Feil is prosecuting the case for the Middle District of Alabama.

An indictment or criminal complaint is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

Reps. Castro, Vasquez, Cisneros Introduce Resolution Recognizing Hispanic and Latino Servicemembers
WASHINGTON, D.C. — Reps. Joaquin Castro (TX-20), Congressional Hispanic Caucus Vice Chair of Diversity and Inclusion, Gabe Vasquez (NM-02), and Gil Cisneros (CA-31) introduced a resolution recognizing the contributions of Hispanic and Latino servicemembers in the United States Armed Forces and calling for stronger Hispanic and Latino leadership across every branch of the military. Between 2017 and 2025, Hispanic representation in the military grew by 6.8 percent, and Hispanic servicemembers now make up 20.81 percent of the force across all branches. They remain underrepresented in leadership. Hispanic servicemembers hold only about 3 percent of general and flag officer positions and less than 10 percent of officer positions in any branch.
“San Antonio, known as Military City, USA, is home to generations of military heroes,” said Congressman Castro. “Latino servicemembers have proudly served in every major war in our nation’s history, and today they are the fastest-growing segment of our armed forces. Yet their contributions have not been equally honored. I’m proud to join Congressman Cisneros in honoring and supporting these servicemembers, and in pushing for leadership that reflects the people who serve.”
“I’m honored to recognize the generations of Latino servicemembers who have served our nation with valor,” said Congressman Cisneros. “But honoring their contributions also means acknowledging the work that needs to be done. While Hispanic and Latino servicemembers account for the largest growing population across the military, they are too often overlooked for leadership roles, and that needs to improve. Our forces are at their best when they reflect our nation’s diversity.”
“The Hispanic community has proudly demonstrated its pride and willingness to serve our nation for decades, diversifying our ranks and strengthening our national defense,” said Congressman Vasquez. “In New Mexico, that tradition runs deep — we are a state of proud Americans who answer the call. This is a reminder that diversity at all ranks makes us stronger as a nation and reflects who we are.”

PIERRE - United States Attorney Ron Parsons announced today that U.S. District Judge Eric C. Schulte has sentenced a Rosebud, South Dakota, woman convicted of Involuntary Manslaughter. The sentencing took place on October 26, 2026.

Crystal McCloskey, age 34, was sentenced to two years and four months in federal prison, followed by three years of supervised release, and ordered to pay a $100 special assessment to the Federal Crime Victims Fund.

McCloskey was indicted by a federal grand jury in January 2026. She pleaded guilty on July 29, 2026.

On June 14, 2025, McCloskey was under the influence of alcohol and controlled substances and drove her vehicle at a high rate of speed. McCloskey missed a curve near Rosebud and drove off the road. The vehicle rolled, throwing McCloskey and her passenger out of the vehicle. The passenger died as a result of her injuries in the crash. The offense occurred in the Rosebud Sioux Indian Reservation.

This matter was prosecuted by the U.S. Attorney’s Office because the Major Crimes Act, a federal statute, mandates that certain violent crimes alleged to have occurred in Indian Country be prosecuted in Federal court as opposed to State court.

This case was investigated by the Rosebud Sioux Tribe Law Enforcement Services, the Oglala Sioux Tribe Department of Public Safety, and the Federal Bureau of Investigation. Assistant U.S. Attorney Kimberly Zachrison prosecuted the case.

McCloskey was ordered to self-surrender to the custody of the U.S. Marshals Service on November 10, 2026.
title: Rosebud Woman Sentenced to Federal Prison for Involuntary Manslaughter

NEWPORT NEWS, Va. – Ex-Enterprise (CVN 65) began its final transit this morning, departing Newport News Shipbuilding for Mobile, Alabama, where the ship will be dismantled.
Commissioned in 1961, the USS Enterprise served the nation for more than 50 years. A technological milestone in naval history, the world’s first nuclear-powered aircraft carrier played a central role in U.S. naval operations during the Cold War, Vietnam War, and post-9/11 conflicts, including Operations Enduring Freedom and Iraqi Freedom.
“Enterprise will always be remembered for her proud legacy of service, a legacy made possible by the Sailors and support personnel whose dedication kept her mission-ready,” said Kevin Cormier, Deputy Portfolio Acquisition Executive Maritime for Aircraft Carriers. “All who served aboard and sustained this historic ship should take pride in the vital role they played in supporting the fleet. Their dedication ensured that Enterprise remained a lasting example of naval excellence. Fair winds and following seas.”
Following Enterprise’s inactivation in December 2012, the Navy completed defueling of the ship’s reactor plants in 2017. Enterprise was decommissioned during a ceremony in the ship’s hangar bay on Feb. 3, 2017. The ceremony marked the end of the ship’s nearly 55-year career and the first decommissioning of a nuclear-powered aircraft carrier.
The eighth naval vessel to bear the name Enterprise, the ship was built by Newport News Shipbuilding and christened Sept. 24, 1960, by Bertha Irene Franke, wife of former Secretary of the Navy William B. Franke. The ship entered service in 1961 and safely steamed more than 1 million nautical miles under nuclear power during its operational career. Enterprise’s legacy will continue with the future Ford-class aircraft carrier, Enterprise (CVN 80), the ninth U.S. Navy ship to carry the name.
The Portfolio Acquisition Executive (PAE) for Maritime is the single accountable organization for delivering surface ships for the U.S. Navy. This centralized organizational construct will empower leaders with broader scope and greater authority to accelerate delivery of combat capability and ensure acquisition speed and discipline are driven by what the warfighter needs—when they need it.
title: Ex-Enterprise (CVN 65) Begins Final Voyage

HOUSTON — ICE officers removed Christian Ruvalcaba-Salas, a 28-year-old criminal illegal alien and accused child rapist, to his home country of Mexico Oct. 16. He was granted conditional permanent resident status by the Biden administration.
“This dangerous criminal alien, who is accused of doing unspeakable things to an innocent child in Mexico, was able to use the immigration status that the Biden administration gave him to allegedly slip into Mexico, brutalize a helpless child and then flee back into the U.S. through the port of entry to evade prosecution,” said ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations Houston Field Office Director Bret Bradford. “That same status then allowed him to remain free in the community for years endangering public safety, despite the fact that he was wanted in Mexico for raping a child and had been arrested for numerous criminal offenses in the U.S. Thankfully, our officers were able to track him down after he attempted to flee and repatriate him to Mexico to face prosecution for his alleged crimes.”
Ruvalcaba-Salas was turned over to Mexican authorities to face prosecution for allegedly raping a child in Aguascalientes, Mexico, in 2022.
Ruvalcaba-Salas has been arrested for numerous crimes in the U.S., including assaulting a peace officer, unlawfully carrying a weapon, criminal trespass and twice for resisting arrest. On July 21, 2025, he pleaded no contest to resisting arrest and received deferred adjudication.
"Criminal illegal aliens who are child predators and sex offenders represent the very worst of the worst and they have no place in the United States,” said ICE Assistant Director of Public Affairs Micah Bock. “ICE will relentlessly pursue these violent predators and remove them, making our communities and neighborhoods safer and more secure.”
Ruvalcaba-Salas was admitted into the U.S. as a nonimmigrant in January 2020, near Laredo. Under the terms of his admission, he was required to leave the U.S. by July 6, 2020, but he failed to depart and remained in the U.S. illegally. On March 4, 2021, the Biden administration granted his petition for conditional permanent resident status. On March 28, 2023, the First Judicial District in the State of Aguascalientes, Mexico, issued a warrant calling for his arrest for allegedly raping a child on Nov. 24, 2022. While the U.S. does not track departures through the ports of entry to Mexico, U.S. Customs and Border Protection encountered him reentering the U.S. three days after the alleged rape on Nov. 27, 2022.
On May 20, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services denied his petition to remove conditions on his residence and terminated his conditional permanent resident status. He was thereafter placed in removal proceedings, and on July 7, an immigration judge ordered him removed from the U.S. in absentia. On Oct. 3, ICE officers successfully tracked him down and took him into custody during a targeted enforcement operation in Giddings.

ATLANTA - Brady Lum, the former chief operating officer of the High Museum of Art, has been sentenced to one year in federal prison for stealing more than $600,000 from the museum by doctoring invoices and approving transactions for personal purchases. Before today’s sentencing hearing, Lum paid full restitution to the museum and reimbursed its $500,000 of investigative expenses and legal fees.

“Lum brazenly pilfered hundreds of thousands of dollars from a beloved civic institution to pay for his high-end guitars and other personal items. His appalling breach of trust damaged not only the High Museum but also the larger art community,” said U.S. Attorney Theodore S. Hertzberg. “Lum repaid the High Museum by covering its losses and expenses, and now he will pay his debt to society from prison.”

“We expect leaders of one of our communities’ historic institutions to serve as stewards, not loot it,” said Marlo Graham, Special Agent in Charge of FBI Atlanta. “Brady Lum manipulated internal processes to steal hundreds of thousands of dollars. The FBI is committed to uncovering and stopping this kind of greed and fraud.”

According to U.S. Attorney Hertzberg, the charges, and other information presented in court: Lum served as the High Museum of Art’s chief operating officer from January 2, 2019, until his resignation on December 9, 2025. Prior to working at the High Museum, Lum held leadership positions at the Coca-Cola Company and Special Olympics International.

During his tenure as the High Museum’s COO, Lum repeatedly purchased non-business items and services for himself, including expensive guitars and other music equipment, personal music lessons, and woodworking equipment, through direct supplier invoicing and the High Museum’s corporate credit card reimbursement process. Lum started to siphon money from the museum in September 2019, less than nine months after he started his COO job, and continued through the discovery of the fraud in November 2025.

Lum concealed the nature of his transactions in several ways, including by submitting altered invoices, using his position to approve expenses, and using accounting adjustments to spread his expenses across different cost centers. Over the course of his scheme, Lum stole more than $600,000 from the High Museum.

Today, U.S. District Judge Michael L. Brown sentenced Brady Lum, 60, of Atlanta, Georgia, to one year in prison to be followed by one year of supervised release. As part of his plea agreement, Lum paid full restitution of $607,688.18 to the High Museum. Lum also voluntarily paid approximately $500,000 to the High Museum to cover costs the museum incurred while uncovering and investigating his criminal activity.

This case was investigated by the Federal Bureau of Investigation.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Nicholas N. Joy prosecuted the case.

For further information please contact the U.S. Attorney’s Public Affairs Office at USAGAN.PressEmails@usdoj.gov or (404) 581-6185. The Internet address for the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Georgia is http://www.justice.gov/usao-ndga .
title: High Museum of Art's Former Chief Operating Officer Sentenced to Federal Prison for Embezzlement

PHILADELPHIA – United States Attorney David Metcalf announced that Donald Michael, aka “Baseball Fun,” 49, of Queen Creek, Arizona, was sentenced to 330 months in prison, 15 years of supervised release, and various financial penalties, including $137,933 in restitution to victims, by United States District Judge Mark A. Kearney for online child sexual exploitation. In addition, Michael is required to register as a sex offender under the Sex Offender Registration and Notification Act and Megan’s Law, as well as state law.

The defendant was charged by indictment in July 2024 with one count of conspiracy to manufacture child pornography, one count of conspiracy to receive and distribute child pornography, one count of distribution and attempted distribution of child pornography, and two counts of receipt of child pornography. He pleaded guilty to all the charges against him in April of last year.

As detailed in court filings and statements, Michael, who served as a baseball coach of minor boys for more than two decades, engaged in an online child exploitation catfishing scheme for over 18 months with co-conspirators Andrew Wolf , a former teacher at Springside Chestnut Hill Academy (“SCH”), and Kray Strange, of Carthage, New York, both of whom were previously convicted and sentenced.

Michael conspired with Wolf and Strange to target minor boys who were Wolf’s current and former students at SCH and to coerce and induce them to produce sexually explicit images and send them to the defendant and his co-conspirators over the internet. They did so by creating multiple fake online profiles where they pretended to be teenaged girls, engaging each of their victims in sexually explicit and graphic chats, and distributing child pornography to the minor boys, in an effort to get them to reciprocate with their own images.

When the boys refused to continue to engage, Michael and his co-conspirators used blackmail and extortion to manipulate them into continuing to produce images. After Wolf and Strange were arrested and incarcerated, this defendant continued his catfishing scheme by targeting and victimizing minor boys who were Little League World Series players.

“Cloaked in the anonymity that the internet provided them, Michael and his co-conspirators manipulated young boys into taking and sending explicit images of themselves,” said U.S. Attorney Metcalf. “These men are predators, plain and simple, and deserve every day of the lengthy sentences they’ve received. Protecting children from sexual exploitation will always be a priority for my office and our partners at the FBI.”

“The sexual exploitation and extortion of children remains one of the most devious crimes the women and men of the FBI investigate,” said Wayne A. Jacobs, Special Agent in Charge of FBI Philadelphia. “This sentencing serves as a reminder how seriously the FBI and our partners take the online victimization of minors. The FBI and our law enforcement partners will continue to work tirelessly to protect young people from exploitation and ensure those who prey on them are brought to justice.”

This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice. Led by United States Attorneys’ Offices and the Criminal Division’s Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to better locate, apprehend, and prosecute individuals who exploit children via the internet, as well as to identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit projectsafechildhood.gov .

The case was investigated by the FBI and prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorneys Kelly Harrell and Michelle Rotella.
title: Arizona Man Sentenced to 27½ Years in Prison for Child Exploitation Offenses in Connection With Catfishing Scheme That Targeted Young Boys

WASHINGTON — The Office of the United States Trade Representative has invoked the Rapid Response Labor Mechanism (RRM) in the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) to review whether workers at Madobox, S.A. de C.V. (Madobox), located in the city of Uruapan in the state of Michoacán, Mexico, are being denied the right to freedom of association and collective bargaining. The U.S. request for review follows an RRM petition received from a Mexican labor union alleging that Madobox is interfering with union activity at the facility. The United States has suspended liquidation of unliquidated entries of goods from the Madobox facility, which produces boxes for commercial use.
Background
The United States Trade Representative (Trade Representative) and the Secretary of Labor co-chair the Interagency Labor Committee for Monitoring and Enforcement (ILC). On September 30, 2026, the Sindicato Nacional de Trabajadores y Empleados de la Industria del Comercio, Alimenticia, Textil, Automotriz, Metalúrgica, Servicios y Distribución “Generalísimo José María Morelos y Pavón”—a Mexican labor union affiliated with the Confederacion Central Nacional (COCENA)—filed a Rapid Response Mechanism (RRM) petition alleging a denial of rights at Madobox. The petition alleges that Madobox is interfering with union activity at the facility, including by unlawfully arranging a collective bargaining agreement (CBA) that was negotiated without workers, by coercing and misinforming workers about the CBA and their union rights, and by unlawfully dismissing workers in retaliation for union activity. The ILC reviews RRM petitions that it receives, and the accompanying information, within 30 days.
After conducting this review, the ILC determined that there is sufficient, credible evidence of a denial of rights enabling the good faith invocation of enforcement mechanisms under the USMCA. As a result, the Trade Representative has submitted a request to Mexico under Annex 31-A of the USMCA that Mexico review whether workers at Madobox are being denied the right to freedom of association and collective bargaining. The Trade Representative has also directed the Secretary of the Treasury to suspend liquidation of unliquidated entries of goods from Madobox.
Mexico has 10 days to agree to conduct a review and, if it agrees, 45 days from today to complete the review.
A copy of the request for review can be found here.
A copy of the letter to the Secretary of the Treasury can be found here.
Information about previous requests can be found here.

title: United States Seeks Mexico’s Review of Alleged Denial of Workers’ Rights at Madobox

- Fully charge all mobile phones, laptops, power banks, medical devices, and any other electronics.

JOINT BASE LEWIS-MCCHORD, Wash. — Leaders from across 1st Special Forces Command (Airborne) gathered at Joint Base Lewis-McChord, Washington, Oct. 26–28, 2026, for a three-day Commanders’ Decision Roundtable focused on talent management, organizational readiness and preparing the force for future operations.
1st Special Forces Group (Airborne) hosted the event, bringing together command teams and staff from across the Special Operations Forces enterprise. On the final day, a central discussion focused on integrating SOF with conventional forces during Large-Scale Combat Operations.
During a leader professional development session, Lt. Gen. Matthew McFarlane, commanding general of I Corps, addressed the growing importance of understanding the theater before crisis occurs, using SOF as the ‘human’ sensor.
“Special Operations Forces inform commanders based on the access and relationships built with partners,” said McFarlane. “SOF is the Joint Force’s primary contact layer with our partners to inform how we see ourselves, the enemy, and the environment.”
1st SFG(A) and I Corps have deliberately strengthened their partnership to improve coordination and develop a more integrated approach to future conflicts. The relationship between 1st SFG(A) and I Corps provides an example of how geographically aligned organizations can build strong working relationships before they are required to operate together in a contested environment.
“1st Special Forces Group’s generational relationships across PACOM remains a key component to their understanding of their assigned area of responsibility,” said Brig. Gen. Joseph Wortham commander if 1st SFC(A). “ There is value in early integration with I Corps in their employment of SOF, to prepare for arguably some of the hardest problem sets.”
McFarlane went on to explain the importance of extending the Joint Force’s reach in theater.
“It is critical that we integrate SOF and partners in Pacific Pathways readiness, building on our more than 40 annual exercises to stress our true joint capability across the challenging and non-contiguous Pacific environment,” he said.
1st SFG(A) regularly participates in exercises with I Corps including Balikatan in the Philippines, Talisman Sabre in Australia, Cobra Gold in Thailand, and Super Garuda Shield in Indonesia.
“Operational preparation of the environment is a shared critical task for both SOF and the conventional force,” said McFarlane. “Understanding the environment from the weather to terrain and the partner force capabilities and capacities is what allows us to build joint interior lines.”
Critically, the leader’s professional development session highlighted the internal SOF integration of Special Forces ‘Green Berets’, Psychological Operations, and Civil Affairs.
“Civil Affairs and Psychological Operations integration with conventional forces is essential,” said McFarlane. “I need your help at echelon to operationalize deception and understand the human environment at a granular level better and faster than our adversary.”
Maj. Gen. Bernard Harrington, commander of the 7th Infantry Division (Multi-Domain Command – Pacific) then spoke with the SOF leaders.
“There’s a lot of synergy between what SOF and 7ID (MDC-PAC) provide to the Joint Force,” said Harrington. “We both set the conditions to best enable the Joint Force commander to accomplish theater-level objectives.”
1st SFG(A) leverages its strategic placement and operational agility as an integralsensor in the joint targeting
chain, providing criticalspecial reconnaissance to the Joint Force.
7ID (MDC-PAC) integrates closely with 1stSFG(A) through collaborative training and mutual innovation in multiple areas including sensing, fires, and autonomy to develop optimal solutions for the Joint Force.
In closing, McFarlane stated, “There has never been a more exciting time to lead in our Army. SOF’s value will be exponentially higher in the next war than the last one, and you play an indispensable role in leading and aligning our efforts to build multidomain dominance for the Joint Force.”
title: I Corps Commander reinforces importance of integration during 1st SFC(A) commanders' decision roundtable

WASHINGTON — Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle traveled to Arkansas, Oct. 29 to 30, to meet with leaders at Pine Bluff Arsenal, Walmart’s corporate headquarters, and the University of Arkansas. Telle’s visit was an opportunity to move from discussion to action as the Army pushes to modernize the defense and organic industrial base, strengthen its global supply chain and build the intellectual and human capital required to ensure the U.S. Army remains the world’s most dominant land force.
The visit connected the Army’s modernization priorities with commercial industry and premier academic institutions. In his recent keynote address at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting, Telle emphasized that the Army must "evolve at the speed of business" and build a "seamless, frictionless, symbiotic relationship with American ingenuity." This trip put that vision into action across the Natural State.
"The forward momentum we saw across Arkansas wouldn't be possible without the leadership and advocacy of President Trump, Secretary of War Hegseth, Senator Boozman, Senator Cotton, Congressman Womack and the entire Arkansas delegation," said Telle. "They are backing our warfighters with the resourcing and legislative firepower needed to modernize our organic industrial base and supercharge our installations. That’s how we empower our Soldiers with every competitive advantage when they step onto the battlefield."
Forging "America’s Arsenal" at Pine Bluff
A key focus of the trip was Pine Bluff Arsenal, a pillar of the Army’s organic industrial base for more than 85 years. PBA provides specialized manufacturing capabilities found nowhere else in the nation. It serves as the nation’s sole-source producer of vital white phosphorus munitions and a primary manufacturer of tactical smoke, pyrotechnics, and illumination rounds. In addition, PBA is a designated Center of Industrial and Technical Excellence for non-lethal ammunition, chemical and biological defense equipment, collective protection filtration, and textile manufacturing.
During his tour of PBA's sprawling 15,000-acre footprint housing over 500 buildings and more than one million square feet of explosive storage, Telle reviewed the facility’s ongoing transformation, which supports the Department of War’s “Arsenal of Freedom” initiative to revitalize America’s defense and organic industrial base.
PBA launched its comprehensive ARSENAL READY campaign last year. The initiative transitions the installation from a reactive sustainment depot into the "Arsenal of Tomorrow" – a continuously loaded, modernized, multi-capability defense industrial park powered by public-private partnerships, expanded enhanced use leasing and portfolio diversification.
"Across the Army – the foundation of the Joint Force – we are committed to rebuilding our military and achieving peace through strength, and that begins right here in Pine Bluff," Telle said. "Pine Bluff Arsenal is 'America’s Arsenal.' What the workforce is doing here to shed legacy acquisition models and transition into a continuously operating, modernized hub is fundamental to Army lethality and our continued dominance on the battlefield."
Unleashing Commercial Logistics in Bentonville
In Bentonville, Telle met with leaders at Walmart’s corporate headquarters and visited their Global Security Operations Center for an open dialogue on how large-scale, globally dispersed enterprises maintain real-time situational awareness, operational resilience and rapid adaptability.
The discussion highlighted how both the Army and the private-sector could share lessons on managing complex global supply chains through natural disasters, dynamic security conditions and emerging global events. Maintaining this continuous operational picture enables organizations to proactively anticipate disruptions, adapt on the fly and surge vital resources to teams in the field – whether supporting communities in times of need or projecting sustainment across complex theaters.
Telle noted that as the Army works to enable endurance as the foundation for the joint force, having open exchanges with private-sector leaders provides invaluable perspectives on supply chain resilience and crisis response. This discussion demonstrated the Army's ongoing drive to engage with and learn from American commercial industry at all levels, adopting best practices that ultimately empower the warfighter.
Advanced Materials, Semiconductor Innovation and Supply Chain Leadership in Fayetteville
The trip concluded in Fayetteville at the University of Arkansas, an academic leader in supply chain management, contested logistics and advanced materials research.
At the university's Engineering Research Center, Telle met with academic leaders and researchers from both the College of Engineering and the College of Business. The dialogue focused on the critical necessity of cultivating future leaders versed in modern supply chain disciplines, expanding cross-sector engagement with industry and leveraging academic expertise to solve complex operational sustainment challenges for the warfighter.
“If we are going to become more efficient, effective and ultimately dominant on the battlefield, we must fully harness what we already have in America, which is the amazing spirit of ingenuity in our entrepreneurial capital markets and world-class research institutions,” Telle said. “We see that on full display here in Northwest Arkansas.”
Telle then visited the university’s Multi-User Silicon Carbide Research and Fabrication Facility, which provides a national platform for advancing silicon carbide semiconductor fabrication and other critical technologies that can enhance next-generation defense systems.
The final stop of the tour was the university's Civil Engineering Research and Education Center, where the group saw cutting-edge advancements in defense-applicable infrastructure and rapid-deployment logistics. They observed a demonstration of CEREC's groundbreaking large-scale structural testing and learned about its pioneering research into 3D-printed structures, fast-setting cement, and other advancements that support a stronger organic industrial base and more resilient supply chains.
"Under the leadership of President Trump and Secretary Hegseth, we are adopting a whole-of-nation approach to defense," Telle said. "From the vital production lines at Pine Bluff, to the global distribution engine of Walmart, to the world-class logistics and materials research at the University of Arkansas, this visit demonstrated the total national ecosystem required to secure our nation. By uniting military capability, private enterprise, and academic innovation, we guarantee the American Soldier is never in a fair fight."
title: Acting Army Secretary visits Arkansas to strengthen industrial base, forge partnerships

GREENEVILLE, Tenn. – On October 29, 2026, Christian Aaron Atkins, 36, of Grainger County, TN was sentenced to 113 months imprisonment by United States District Judge, the Honorable Clifton L. Corker, in the United States District Court at Greeneville. Following his imprisonment, Atkins will be on supervised release for five years.

Earlier this year, Atkin’s four co-conspirators, Tonya Renee Valentine, 44, Karen E. Carpenter, 48, Donald Eugene Roberts, 48, and Jacob Adam Parkey, 41, also of Grainger County, were sentenced by Judge Corker. Following their terms of imprisonment, all co-conspirators will be on supervised release for five years.

Each co-conspirators signed plea agreements and pleaded guilty to a conspiracy to distribute 50 grams or more of methamphetamine, in violation of 21 U.S.C. § 846, 841(a)(1), and 841(b)(1)(A).

According to plea agreements filed in the case, the Bean Station Police Department, in coordination with the Federal Bureau of Investigation High-Intensity Drug Trafficking Area Task Force (FBI HIDTA), conducted a lengthy and targeted narcotics investigation involving multiple individuals engaged in the distribution of methamphetamine in the region. Throughout the course of the investigation, agents seized approximately 1,200 grams of methamphetamine and executed three separate search warrants, which resulted in the additional seizure of approximately 2 pounds of methamphetamine. Agents also seized $4,864.00 in U.S. currency believed to be proceeds of illegal narcotics distribution.

On June 3, 2026, Valentine was sentenced to 180 months imprisonment.

On June 25, 2026, Roberts was sentenced to 120 months imprisonment.

On August 12, 2026, Carpenter was sentenced to 120 months imprisonment.

On August 19, 2026, Parkey was sentenced to 126 months imprisonment.

U.S. Attorney Francis M. Hamilton III of the Eastern District of Tennessee, and Special Agent in Charge Terrence G. Riley, of the Nashville Field Office’s Knoxville Resident Agency, made the announcement.

The case was the result of an investigation by the Bean Station Police Department and the FBI HIDTA Task Force.

Assistant United States Attorney Andrew C. Parker represented the United States in this case.

This case is part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of United States law enforcement towards identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States.

###
title: Five Grainger County Residents Sentenced In Methamphetamine Trafficking Ring

RELEASE: Gottheimer Joins Darren Drake Foundation, Drake Family for Darren Drake Memorial
Honors Life of Darren Drake on Ninth Anniversary of Terror Attack
Above: Gottheimer at Darren Drake Memorial.
NEW MILFORD, NJ — Congressman Josh Gottheimer (NJ-5) joined the Darren Drake Foundation and the Drake family at New Milford High School for a special memorial flag-raising ceremony to commemorate the life of Darren Drake and highlight Gottheimer’s bipartisan Darren Drake Act, which was signed into law to help combat lone-wolf terror attacks.
Watch Gottheimer’s full remarks here.
“It’s hard to believe that it’s been nine years since New Milford and the Drakes lost Darren. A blink of an eye. Yet, as we promised then, we would always honor Darren’s memory. This community has never forgotten,” said Congressman Josh Gottheimer (NJ-5). “The Darren Drake Act has become an essential tool in our arsenal to eradicate terrorist threats in our country. And, it exists because of Jimmy and Barbara – and Darren.”
Gottheimer’s bipartisan Darren Drake Act, signed into law in December 2022, helps stop terrorists from easily acquiring trucks and other vehicles to use as weapons in attacks. Working closely with vehicle rental companies and in consultation with federal, state, and local law enforcement, the legislation requires the U.S. Department of Homeland Security to take concrete steps to stop known terrorists from renting vehicles.
On October 31, 2017, Darren was murdered in a terrorist attack while on a New York City bike path, where he was deliberately run down by an ISIS sympathizer in a rented pickup truck. The Darren Drake Foundation was created to honor his legacy and pursue the ideals and vision he was so passionate about.
Gottheimer was joined by Mayor Michael Putrino, Councilman Matthew Seymour, and Councilman Arthur Zeilner.

Wanted Fugitive Tracked to Dominica, Arrested and Extradited Back to the Virgin Islands After Almost Two Years on the Run
For immediate release
Rashawn Abraham, Deputy U.S. Marshal
ST. THOMAS, V.I. – A St. Thomas man wanted for 12 firearm and drug related charges apprehended in Dominica and extradited to the Virgin Islands by the U.S. Marshals Service (USMS).
Jahi Grant, 46, wanted by the Virgin Islands Police Department (VIPD) for multiple charges, including possession of an unlicensed machine gun, assault on a law enforcement officer and possession with intent to distribute controlled substances, was arrested on Aug. 27 in Dominica by the Commonwealth of Dominica Police Force (CDPF).
Grant’s charges stem from a Dec. 2024 incident, where a machine gun and pistol were recovered. Grant fled the scene and a warrant was subsequently issued for his arrest in Jan. 2025.
On Jan. 14, 2025, the VIPD requested the assistance of the U.S. Marshals Florida/Caribbean Regional Fugitive Task Force in the District of the Virgin Islands in locating and apprehending Grant.
Through investigative efforts, community assistance and VIPD and USMS collaboration, it was revealed that Grant fled St. Thomas and was residing in Dominica. With the support of the USMS Jamaican Foreign Field Office, contact was made with the CDPF, alerting them to intel indicating Grant’s presence in Dominica and his active warrants out of the Virgin Islands.
On Oct. 19, 2026, CDPF Task Force members confirmed seeing Grant. He was taken into custody on Oct. 27, by the CDPF and officially deported and extradited back to the Virgin Islands by U.S. Marshals on Oct. 30.
Once arriving in St. Thomas, Grant was turned over to the VIPD and booked in the Virgin Islands Bureau of Corrections.
“This successful operation highlights the strength of our law enforcement partnerships throughout the Caribbean, “ said Kwesi R. Howard, U.S. Marshal of the District of the Virgin Islands. “I commend the Commonwealth of Dominica Police Force for their professionalism and cooperation in helping return this fugitive to the Virgin Islands. Working alongside the VIPD and our regional partners, we remain committed to ensuring that those who flee justice are held accountable.”
title: Wanted Fugitive Tracked to Dominica, Arrested and Extradited Back to the Virgin Islands After Almost Two Years on the Run | U.S. Marshals Service

text:
On All Saints’ Day, I join Christians across our Nation in honoring the men and women through the centuries whose extraordinary lives of faithfulness reveal the great goodness and love to which human beings can aspire.
Every generation of Americans has understood the profound power of the example of a heroic and holy life, which is why the names of saints are so interwoven throughout the American landscape. We have San Francisco, California, named for Saint Francis of Assisi; San Antonio, Texas, named for Saint Anthony of Padua; St. Louis, Missouri, named for a saintly king of France; and St. Paul, Minnesota, named for the great Apostle. From Santa Monica, California, to St. Augustine, Florida, saints greet us on maps and road signs across the country.
Saints are just as present in the institutions we know and trust. Families turn to St. Jude Children’s Research Hospital when a child is gravely ill. Young Americans study at Saint John’s University, Saint Louis University, Saint Bonaventure University, and many other colleges and universities named for saints. Every March, millions of Americans celebrate Saint Patrick’s Day with parades, music, and the wearing of green.
Even our professional sports carry this legacy. When New Orleans received its National Football League franchise on November 1, 1966, the date was no accident: It was All Saints’ Day. A local businessman championed the name “Saints,” inspired by the city’s celebrated jazz anthem, “When the Saints Go Marching In.”
From sea to shining sea, these names are a constant reminder that a great civilization needs more than material success. It needs examples of goodness. It needs heroes not only of strength and achievement but also of mercy, sacrifice, humility, and love.
In the United States, we especially honor Saint Junípero Serra, who carried the Christian faith through the missions of California; Saint Elizabeth Ann Seton, who helped build Catholic education in America; Saint Katharine Drexel, who devoted her fortune and her life to educating and serving poor and impoverished communities; and Saint Frances Xavier Cabrini, who established schools, orphanages, and hospitals, putting Christian charity into action and bringing the hope of Jesus to those most in need. Countless other saints—parents, teachers, nurses, workers, missionaries, and neighbors whose names history never recorded—quietly showed what holiness can look like in ordinary life.
All Saints’ Day proclaims a truth at the heart of the Christian faith: Death does not have the final word. Christians believe that through the death and Resurrection of Jesus Christ, the grave has been conquered and eternal life has been opened to all who believe in Him. The saints are witnesses to that promise. We honor them not merely as heroes of the past but also as signs of the hope that extends to every human life and reaches beyond our earthly existence.
On this All Saints’ Day, Melania and I offer our warmest greetings to all who observe this holy feast. I will always defend the freedom of Americans to express their faith openly and without fear. May the lives of the saints renew our gratitude for our Nation’s spiritual inheritance; strengthen our resolve to love and serve one another; and inspire us to live with the faith, courage, and charity that make a people—and a nation—forever great.
title: Presidential Message on All Saints’ Day

Coast Guard Southwest District interdicts 37 aliens off California, between Oct. 5-30
U.S. Coast Guard Southwest District Public Affairs: (206) 815-6689
SAN DIEGO — The Coast Guard apprehended 37 aliens off the coast of Southern California between Oct. 5 and 30.
On Oct. 9, a Coast Guard Maritime Safety and Security Team (MSST) boatcrew interdicted 13 suspected aliens aboard a 24-foot vessel approximately 7 miles off San Diego. The individuals were transferred to the custody of Imperial Beach Border Patrol agents at Ballast Point.
Later that same day, Coast Guard Sector Los Angeles-Long Beach watchstanders received notification that the crew of the Coast Guard Cutter Narwhal (WPB 87335) interdicted 23 suspected aliens aboard a 25-foot cuddy-cabin vessel near Santa Cruz Island while on patrol.
The Narwhal crew transported the suspected aliens to Coast Guard Base Los Angeles-Long Beach, where they were transferred to U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP).  A Coast Guard Station Channel Islands crew seized the vessel and transferred it to CBP.
On Oct. 17, Coast Guard watchstanders detected a suspicious personal watercraft (PWC) traveling at high speed off Point Loma and diverted an MSST Honolulu boatcrew to investigate. When the operator failed to comply with the crew’s commands, a pursuit ensued, and Coast Guard PWCs were diverted to the pursuit to assist.
The vessel struck a wave and capsized during the pursuit. The boatcrew apprehended the passenger, while the operator swam ashore and evaded authorities.
The Coast Guard works closely with federal and international partners to disrupt human smuggling operations and ensure the safety of those at sea. Maritime smuggling attempts are inherently dangerous and often involve overloaded, unseaworthy vessels.
“These operations and interdictions reflect the Coast Guard’s persistent, multi-mission presence throughout Southern California’s maritime region,” said Coast Guard Capt. Jason Hagen, Southwest District chief of enforcement. “Our crews stand ready to conduct border security operations, enforce federal laws, and keep our waters safe. Dangerous and illegal migration attempts place lives at risk, especially when smugglers use overcrowded, poorly equipped vessels not suited for ocean conditions.”
-USCG-
title: Coast Guard Southwest District interdicts 37 aliens off California, between Oct. 5-30

text:
ASTANA, Kazakhstan – Two female freestyle wrestlers from the U.S. Army World Class Athlete Program embodied readiness and resiliency for Team USA during the United World Wrestling Senior World Championships.
And they played an important part of helping Team USA secure its first world championship for the first time since 1999 by edging powerhouse Japan, 137-135.
Spc. Adaugo Nwachukwu became the first WCAP Soldier-athlete to win a world championship since 2005 in a 12-11 thriller at 62 kilograms on Oct. 29 against two-time world champion and 2024 Olympic bronze medalist Nonoka Ozaki of Japan.
Sgt. Abby Nette dropped an 8-6 heartbreaker to India’s Manisha Bhanwala to earn a silver medal at 59 kilograms. Nwachukwu and Nette are the first women’s freestyle wrestlers in Army WCAP to win medals in the same world championships.
“I have a saying: ‘We’re not here to take part. We’re here to take over,’ ” said Bruce Robinson, Army WCAP women’s freestyle coach who assisted Team USA. “I say it jokingly but, at the same time. I’m not joking because I know the potential these women have. When they come into this program and develop the mindset that comes with being part of the military, it adds another layer to what they’re capable of doing.”
The success of Nwachukwu and Nette during the senior world championships also spotlights the opportunities WCAP offers aspiring leaders who want to compete at the international and Olympic level while serving the nation.
“The success has elevated the program,” Robinson said. “Everybody’s talking about WCAP now. I’ve gotten so many texts and messages from college coaches and wrestlers saying, ‘WCAP is killing it. What are you all doing?’ They see that WCAP produced two of the three finalists. Not everybody can say that. The entire year has been incredible, from having Pan American champions to having six make the finals at the U.S. Open.”
To cap off the incredible year, former WCAP stalwart Iris Smith will be inducted into the Nationnal Wrestling Hall of Fame.
The championship culture fostered under Robinson and assistant Nate Engel isn’t lost on Terry Steiner, head women’s freestyle wrestling coach for Team USA.
“They really transformed the program, and I’m glad to have Army WCAP as part of Team USA,” said Steiner, who has served as Team USA’s coach since 2004. “I can’t say enough about their leadership and what they have done.”
While winning the world championship is gratifying and a huge accomplishment, it’s not surprising, Nette said.
“This has been a long time coming, but at the same time, it just makes us hungry for more,” she said. “This is the first team title in 27 years, but it won’t be the last. Hopefully next year we continue building on it and keep setting the standard.”
Nwachukwu, the third seed, opened her tournament with two straight victories by technical superiority – defined as victories by a margin greater than 10 points – against Turkey’s Sevim Akbas and Sweden’s Sara Lindborg.
Nwachukwu beat Bulgaria’s Bilyana Dudova, ranked second in the world, 5-2 to punch her ticket to her first senior world final.
In the final, Nwachukwu stormed out to a 4-0 lead and led 9-4 at one point, but Ozaki scored seven straight points. Nwachukwu, who earned a silver medal in the Under-23 world championships almost two weeks ago in Las Vegas, overcame fatigue to score a takedown in the waning seconds.
The victory capped off a remarkable two weeks for Nwachukwu.
“I knew with U23 worlds and senior worlds so close together that I had signed up for a challenge,” Nwachukwu said. “Obviously, U23s didn’t go the way I wanted, but I had to leave that in the past. I knew I could win at that level, and I knew I was capable of winning senior worlds. I just kept telling myself to let go of the past and wrestle like it was my last opportunity.”
Nette, seeded fifth, also had a remarkable run. She opened with a pin over Burundi’s Gloria Niyonkuru, edged Russia’s Svetlana Lipatova 7-6, and pinned Ukraine’s Mariia Vynnyk, ranked No. 1 in the world, in the semifinals.
In her final, she led 6-0, but a questionable call changed the match’s momentum. That shift stressed the importance of having the proper mental mindset, Nette said.
“I had the match in the palm of my hand,” Nette said. “Watching Adaugo compete this past year and seeing how locked in she has been has shown me just how important that mental side is.”
As long as Nette and Nwachukwu are part of the program, something special is always going to happen, Engel said.
“These two are perfect examples of serving their country, competing at the highest level, and accomplishing great things,” he said.
Both Nette and Nwachukwu stressed it’s a privilege to compete at the highest level while serving.
“Whenever I’m working with kids, I tell then how fortunate I am to be able to do what I love while serving my country,” Nwachukwu said. “The Army provides countless opportunities.”
Nette echoed that sentiment.
“We get to represent the United States both as Soldiers and athletes,” she said. “That’s a really special feeling.”
The Army WCAP Greco-Roman team also had four Soldier-athletes compete for Team USA in the senior worlds. Sgt. Kamal Bey (82 kilograms) lost to China’s Halishan Bahejiang, 4-2; Sgt. Dalton Roberts (60 kilograms) lost to Romania’s Razvan Arnaut by technical superiority, 9-0; and Spc. Timothy Young (97 kilograms) lost to Croatia’s Matej Mandic, 4-3.
All were eliminated when their opponents failed to reach their respective finals.
title: US Army wrestlers help Team USA capture first world title since 1999
